sections.title: Why don’t the pipes clog completely?
sections.text:
Why don’t the pipes clog completely? 
           They are maintained regularly. Pigging scrubs away marine growth before it can seriously restrict flow. 
           Why use natural seawater? 
           Natural Monterey Bay seawater helps recreate local marine conditions and supports exhibits connected to the bay ecosystem. 
           What are the orange cylinders? 
           They are pipeline pigs — large foam scrubbers pushed through pipes by water pressure. 
           Does upwelling affect the Aquarium? 
           Yes. Upwelling increases nutrients and productivity in the bay, which can also increase growth in seawater pipes. 
           Is all water the same for every exhibit? 
           No. Different animals and exhibits may need different temperatures, flow, filtration, lighting, and water quality conditions.

sections.title: Identification and range
sections.text: Identification and range Also known as bluespotted lagoon ray. Bright blue spots mark a yellow-green disc, and a whip-like tail bears venomous serrated spines. Reported disc width 12–14 in, total length up to 28 in. Indo-Pacific and coastal Indian Ocean, typically shallow water to 66 ft.

sections.title: Habitat and behavior
sections.text: Habitat and behavior Adults are associated with coral reefs, resting beneath ledges or in caves by day and foraging at night in reef and sand habitats. Juveniles use sheltered shallow habitats such as seagrass beds and mangroves. Cleaner wrasses may remove parasites.

sections.title: Diet and sensory adaptations
sections.text: Diet and sensory adaptations Crustaceans, mollusks and polychaete worms are located with sensitive ampullae of Lorenzini. Crushing dental plates process hard-shelled prey; spiracles assist breathing while resting.

sections.title: Reproduction
sections.text: Reproduction Males have paired claspers. Females give birth to live young, typically reported as 2–7 pups; the source describes variable gestation of 4–12 months. Spot patterns can help distinguish individuals.

sections.title: Why the spots look blue
sections.text: Why the spots look blue The striking blue is structural rather than a conventional blue pigment: nanoscale structures beneath the skin reflect blue light, while deeper pigmented layers absorb other wavelengths. The source references microscopic studies of the skin.

sections.title: Conservation and visitor interpretation
sections.text: Conservation and visitor interpretation The shift update lists the species as Least Concern and lifespan as unknown. Do not touch the ray or its venomous tail spines. Some proposed functions of its blue spots, such as warning coloration, remain hypotheses.

sections.title: Quick Facts
sections.text: Quick Facts Length Mixed claims: 16–19 in maximum Diet Zooplankton Predators Pinnipeds, dolphins, seabirds, larger fish, large squid Depth Typically 0–35 ft; source says never below the photic zone Habitat Nearshore open waters; eggs along rocky shores near kelp forests Status Least Concern (IUCN), per source The source describes this as the California subspecies of Bennett’s flying fish,  Cheilopogon pinnatibarbatus , and the largest of the flying fishes. It connects increasing California sightings with warmer water, marine heatwaves and El Niño events. A generic body plan for the Cheilopogon fishes.

sections.title: Life Cycle & Reproduction
sections.text: Life Cycle & Reproduction The source describes a simple oviparous life cycle: eggs, larval development, fry and mature adults. Females use sticky filaments to attach eggs to substrate and macroalgae, often around kelp beds. The source does not specify clutch size for this fish, but notes related species commonly lay roughly 20,000–50,000 eggs. Juveniles may take a year or two to reach maturity.

sections.title: Gliding — Not True Flight
sections.text: Gliding — Not True Flight Modified pectoral fins function as airfoils. The source presents predator evasion as a leading explanation for the adaptation and describes a fight-or-glide response. It reports that sufficiently warm water—around 68°F—helps the fish build launch speed, with movement around 22 mph and sometimes faster under favorable wind conditions. Flying fish use speed, enlarged fins and tail-assisted taxiing to extend a glide.

sections.title: Launch, Taxi, Glide & Re-entry
sections.text: Launch, Taxi, Glide & Re-entry In the water the pectoral fins remain tucked against the body to reduce drag. For launch, the fish accelerates, often uses a swell and its associated lift, then taxis with the tail while the body is airborne. It eventually loses momentum or ends the glide and returns to the ocean. The source compares its relatively high wing/fin loading with birds such as cormorants. Swimming → leaping and fin deployment → taxiing → gliding → water re-entry.

sections.title: Fin Development & Genetics
sections.text: Fin Development & Genetics The source includes an infographic describing research into a conserved transporter-protein gene and amino-acid changes that may contribute to unusual fin proportions in flying fishes and relatives. Infographic supplied with the Naturalist update on possible gene changes associated with flying-fish fin proportions.

sections.title: Eyes for Water and Air
sections.text: Eyes for Water and Air The source describes pyramid-shaped corneas with three windows and notes that researchers are still investigating their function. The proposed advantage is useful vision across both underwater and aerial environments while tracking predators, judging swells and transitioning between water and air.

sections.title: Skeleton & Control
sections.text: Skeleton & Control The source describes fused vertebrae in the tail for rigidity, reinforcement between the spine and cranium, and a thick jawbone that may help withstand water re-entry. The fish cannot steer like a bird but can make small course adjustments during a glide.

sections.title: Fisheries & Conservation
sections.text: Fisheries & Conservation The source reports no large-scale commercial fishery for California flying fish, though they may be caught as bait for large pelagic fishes in California. Bennett’s flying fish and other flying fishes are harvested elsewhere. The update states that no flying-fish species is currently known to be endangered because of fishery pressure.

sections.title: In 30 Seconds ⌄
sections.text: In 30 Seconds ⌄ California sheephead are large wrasses of rocky reefs and kelp forests. Their strong teeth and throat plates break hard-shelled prey. Adults may change from female to male, and by feeding on sea urchins, they can help maintain kelp-forest balance.

sections.title: Quick Facts ⌄
sections.text: Quick Facts ⌄ Family Labridae — wrasses Exhibit Kelp Forest Range Monterey Bay to the Sea of Cortez; uncommon north of Point Conception Size Up to about 3 ft (91 cm), 36 lb (16.3 kg) Diet Sea urchins, crabs, lobsters, mollusks and other hard-shelled animals

sections.title: Identification ⌄
sections.text: Identification ⌄ Mature males have a dark head and tail, reddish-orange middle, white chin, red eyes, and often a pronounced forehead bump. Females are generally more uniformly pink. Large canine teeth help identify the species; juveniles look different from both adult forms.

sections.title: Feeding and Teeth ⌄
sections.text: Feeding and Teeth ⌄ A sheephead uses protruding canine teeth to pry hard-shelled invertebrates from rocks. Its jaws break apart prey, and modified throat bones further grind shell fragments. This combination makes it an effective predator on sea urchins and shellfish.

sections.title: Sex Change and Reproduction ⌄
sections.text: Sex Change and Reproduction ⌄ California sheephead are protogynous: individuals first mature as females, and some later become males. The timing of transition varies with local conditions and population structure. Removing large males can influence social structure, so sex-changing life history is important in fisheries management. Female California sheephead transitioning toward male coloration. Photograph preserved from an earlier Naturalist Field Note.

sections.title: Day and Night Behavior ⌄
sections.text: Day and Night Behavior ⌄ Active during daylight, sheephead search rocky reefs and kelp forests for prey. At night they shelter in crevices or caves and may envelop themselves in a mucus cocoon. The Aquarium describes this coating as helping obscure the fish’s scent from nighttime predators.

sections.title: Kelp Forest Connections ⌄
sections.text: Kelp Forest Connections ⌄ Sheephead consume sea urchins, which graze kelp. By reducing urchin pressure, predators such as sheephead can help support healthy kelp forests. This effect depends on the broader food web and local ecological conditions.

sections.title: Conservation ⌄
sections.text: Conservation ⌄ The Aquarium documents changes in sheephead fishing pressure and California fishing regulations enacted in 2002 to help limit overfishing. The Aquarium species page describes the species as Vulnerable under IUCN; conservation assessments and regulations can change, so check current sources when advising visitors.

sections.title: Scientific Name and Taxonomy ⌄
sections.text: Scientific Name and Taxonomy ⌄ The Monterey Bay Aquarium species page currently uses  Semicossyphus pulcher . A February 2026 Naturalist Field Note reports the alternative combination  Bodianus pulcher . Taxonomic sources are not fully consistent in their naming; both names refer to California sheephead. This guide retains the Aquarium’s displayed name while documenting the alternative.

sections.title: Life Cycle & Reproduction
sections.text: Life Cycle & Reproduction Breeding depends on suitable environmental conditions, including food availability and water quality. Males compete for territories with protected sites suitable for egg laying and display to females with dynamic bands of color. Cuttlefish mate face-to-face. The male transfers spermatophores (sperm packets) to the female. A female may attach roughly 5–25 fertilized eggs to hard substrate in a protected den. She tends the eggs, including circulating water around them, and the eggs may hatch in about 30 days. Newly hatched juveniles resemble miniature adults and are ready to hunt soon after hatching.

sections.title: Hunting & Feeding
sections.text: Hunting & Feeding Like squid, cuttlefish have eight arms plus two specialized feeding tentacles. The tentacles can shoot outward beyond the body to seize prey and then retract toward the beak. Flamboyant cuttlefish can produce moving bands of color while approaching prey. Their remarkably rapid appearance changes are produced by specialized skin structures controlled by the nervous system.

sections.title: Why Do They “Walk”?
sections.text: Why Do They “Walk”? Although capable of swimming, flamboyant cuttlefish are frequently observed moving along the seafloor using their arms in a distinctive walking or strutting motion. Cuttlefish possess an internal shell called a  cuttlebone . In this species the cuttlebone is relatively small and narrow compared with many other cuttlefish, providing less buoyancy assistance. Moving along the bottom may therefore be less energetically costly than sustained swimming.

sections.title: Color Change & Camouflage
sections.text: Color Change & Camouflage Cephalopod skin combines several specialized structures: Chromatophores  — pigment-containing organs that expand and contract. Iridophores  — reflective structures containing crystalline material that produce iridescent effects. Leucophores  — structures that reflect ambient light. Papillae  — muscular skin structures that can alter the texture of the body surface. Together these systems allow rapid camouflage, communication and conspicuous displays.

sections.title: Anatomy
sections.text: Anatomy 8 arms + 2 specialized feeding tentacles Beak and radula Internal cuttlebone Ink sac Three hearts: one systemic heart and two branchial hearts associated with the gills Large central brain plus extensive neural processing within the arms Distinctive W-shaped pupils Much of a cephalopod's nervous system extends outside the central brain. Large concentrations of neurons in the arms allow substantial local sensory processing and motor control. This is the origin of the popular—but simplified—description of cephalopods as having “nine brains.”

sections.title: Intelligence & Senses
sections.text: Intelligence & Senses Cuttlefish have large and sophisticated nervous systems for invertebrates. Experiments have demonstrated abilities including learning, discrimination of small quantities and delayed gratification under laboratory conditions. Their distinctive W-shaped pupils are part of a highly developed visual system. Cuttlefish do not perceive color the way humans do, but they can detect polarized light and contrast extremely well.

sections.title: Poison & Warning Colors
sections.text: Poison & Warning Colors Flamboyant cuttlefish are notable because their tissues contain  tetrodotoxin (TTX) , making them poisonous if eaten. Their vivid appearance may function as  aposematic coloration —a visual warning to potential predators. Useful visitor distinction:  poisonous organisms cause harm when eaten or contacted; venomous organisms actively deliver toxins through structures such as bites or stings. The flamboyant cuttlefish is described as poisonous, whereas blue-ringed octopuses use venom during a bite.

sections.title: Biomimicry & the Cuttlebone
sections.text: Biomimicry & the Cuttlebone Cuttlebone combines low weight with an intricate chambered architecture. It is largely composed of aragonite and must tolerate substantial pressure while maintaining the animal's buoyancy. Researchers have studied cuttlebone architecture as inspiration for lightweight structures capable of handling compression and thermal stresses. Such biological designs are of interest for advanced engineering, including aerospace applications.

sections.title: Monterey Bay Aquarium Connection
sections.text: Monterey Bay Aquarium Connection Flamboyant cuttlefish were previously displayed at Monterey Bay Aquarium in  Tentacles . They are returning with  Ocean in Motion . The Aquarium has previous experience culturing this species, and new generations have been raised behind the scenes as aquarists prepare for the exhibit.

sections.title: Guide Talking Points
sections.text: Guide Talking Points Why does it walk? Its small cuttlebone provides relatively little buoyancy, so moving along the bottom may cost less energy than swimming. Can it really change color? Yes. Chromatophores and reflective skin structures allow extremely rapid changes used for camouflage, communication and hunting displays. Is it venomous? It is better described as poisonous: its tissues contain tetrodotoxin. Blue-ringed octopuses, by comparison, deliver venom with a bite. Does it really have nine brains? Not literally. It has one central brain, but a large amount of neural processing occurs in the arms, which can perform sophisticated local sensory and motor processing. Why is the pupil shaped like a W? The unusual pupil is part of a highly specialized visual system adapted to detecting contrast and polarized light. What is a cuttlebone? It is the cuttlefish's internal shell. In many cuttlefish it helps regulate buoyancy.

sections.title: What Makes It Different?
sections.text: What Makes It Different? Gooseneck or leaf barnacles do not resemble the familiar volcano-shaped acorn barnacles. Adults retain a flexible stalk, or peduncle, rather than being enclosed in a rigid cone-shaped shell. They commonly occur in dense clusters, or rosettes, and may live among California mussels on wave-swept rocky shores.

sections.title: Life Cycle & Settlement
sections.text: Life Cycle & Settlement Like other barnacles, gooseneck barnacles pass through two pelagic larval forms before settling: the feeding  nauplius  stage and the non-feeding  cyprid  stage. When ready to settle, cement glands connect through a cement duct at the base of the peduncle and effectively glue the animal to hard substrate. Settling near other members of the species is important for cross-fertilization. Maturity is described in the source Field Note as occurring around five years. A mature individual may release roughly 20,000 eggs per brood and may produce several broods in a year.

sections.title: Anatomy
sections.text: Anatomy The adult consists of a flexible  peduncle (stalk)  attached to the substrate and a capitulum containing the feeding and major body structures. The source material highlights the mouth, cirri, digestive system, cement glands and duct, nervous system, and both male and female reproductive structures.

sections.title: Feeding & Life in the Surf
sections.text: Feeding & Life in the Surf Rather than resisting every wave with a rigid shell, the flexible stalk allows a gooseneck barnacle to move with heavy surge. The animal can orient toward water flow and extend its  cirri  to capture plankton and suspended organic material. Barnacle cirri are modified appendages. Fine structures trap material from the water; captured material is moved toward the mouth, where the animal can distinguish useful organic material from non-food particles.

sections.title: Reproduction & Rosettes
sections.text: Reproduction & Rosettes Gooseneck barnacles are commonly packed closely together. The Field Note connects this tight clustering with the need for neighboring animals to cross-fertilize. Their reproductive anatomy does not provide the extreme reach associated with some other barnacles, so close neighbors are especially useful.

sections.title: Fluorescence
sections.text: Fluorescence Gooseneck barnacles fluorescing under ultraviolet light. Image credited in the source Field Note to Peter Tannas.

sections.title: People, Harvest & Food
sections.text: People, Harvest & Food Gooseneck barnacles have long been harvested and eaten by Indigenous peoples along the North Pacific coast from Central California north to British Columbia. A European relative,  Pollicipes pollicipes , is a highly valued food around the Iberian Peninsula. The Field Note emphasizes that harvesting can be difficult and the product degrades quickly, contributing to high prices. It also notes that commercial harvest in parts of the Pacific Northwest and Vancouver region is regulated to reduce overharvesting.

sections.title: Guide Talking Points
sections.text: Guide Talking Points Is it really a crustacean? Yes. Despite its unusual adult form, it is a crustacean and has free-swimming larval stages. What are the feathery structures? They are cirri—modified appendages used to filter food from moving water. Why are they packed together? Dense groups help them occupy favorable wave-swept habitat and keep potential reproductive partners close. How do they stay attached? Cement glands and a cement duct at the base of the stalk produce the attachment system used during settlement. Can people eat them? Yes. Gooseneck barnacles have a long history as food and remain commercially harvested in some regions.

sections.title: January 2026 Gray Whale Migration
sections.text: January 2026 Gray Whale Migration By early February, the southbound migration was slowing and some juvenile gray whales were already heading north. Fourteen cow–calf pairs were reported passing Southern California, mostly in healthy condition. The 2025–26 season ended January at approximately 130 sightings, compared with around 80 in 2024–25 and a nine-season average near 390. Counts improved over the previous season but remained far below the historical average. These are monitoring counts, not a full population census. Juveniles sometimes reverse direction before reaching the Baja California breeding grounds. Cow–calf pairs generally travel north later.

sections.title: Gray Whale Ecology & Conservation — January 2026
sections.text: Gray Whale Ecology & Conservation — January 2026 For visitors:  Gray whales migrate past Monterey Bay in winter. They are unusual among baleen whales because they often feed by suctioning prey from the seafloor, stirring sediment as they go. Reports of plump-looking migrants in January 2026 were encouraging, but do not by themselves prove population recovery. Migration, reproduction and calves Eastern North Pacific gray whales generally travel between northern feeding grounds and calving areas near Baja California. Gestation is approximately 12–13 months; calves are born large and grow rapidly on rich milk. Mothers and calves usually head north later than other adults. Breeding groups may include one female and several males. Feeding, whale riders and ecosystem engineering Gray whales consume amphipods and other small animals, often by rolling onto a side, suctioning sediment and filtering prey with baleen. Feeding disturbs the seafloor, creating pits and redistributing sediment. Specialized gray whale barnacles ( Cryptolepas rhachianecti ) and whale lice (cyamids) live on their bodies. Some individuals preferentially feed on one side, leaving asymmetric barnacle wear. Their diet can also include other crustaceans and prey in different habitats. Population decline and unusual mortality events NOAA designated an eastern North Pacific gray whale unusual mortality event from December 2018 through November 2023. Hundreds of strandings were documented. Poor body condition, reduced prey availability and changing Arctic ecosystems are major concerns, while vessel strikes and entanglements remain threats. The exact contributions of environmental and human pressures are still being studied; do not attribute the event to an unsupported single cause. Population abundance estimates, calf counts and local whale-watching sightings measure different things and should not be treated as interchangeable. The Pacific Coast Feeding Group is a distinct feeding aggregation within the eastern North Pacific population. sections.title: 📖 Steve Webster's Story
sections.text: 📖 Steve Webster's Story A 26-foot-long, young-of-the-year male gray whale washed ashore near the Seaside sewage treatment plant. Steve Webster and colleagues decided to recover its skeleton. Three tow trucks were brought in to move the whale, but the team had to wait for a marine mammal permit before flensing could begin. In the September warmth, decomposition gases built up inside the carcass. The team warned everyone to avoid cutting the body cavity, but someone miscalculated. The carcass ruptured, sending a geyser of hot, putrid blood about 20 feet into the air. People holding long flensing knives scattered. Steve compared the scene to a cheap samurai movie. Julie Packard was present wearing a white sweatshirt; astonishingly, not a drop of blood touched it. The bones were buried on the beach at the Naval Postgraduate School, recovered about a year later, cleaned at a car wash, and soaked in Biz enzyme detergent for approximately six months to remove oil. The bones were then stabilized with vinylite resin and reassembled with advice from Vic Morejohn of Moss Landing Marine Laboratories. Years later, a veterinary pathologist noticed osteochondrosis dissecans in the shoulder joints. Steve suggested the condition may have interfered with the whale's migration and contributed to starvation. No obvious net damage or other trauma had been found.

sections.title: ❓ Visitor Questions
sections.text: ❓ Visitor Questions What whale is this?  A young-of-the-year male gray whale, about 26 feet long. Where was it found?  On the beach near the Seaside sewage treatment plant. How did the Aquarium prepare the skeleton?  The team recovered and flensed the carcass, buried the bones for about a year, cleaned and degreased them, stabilized them with resin, and reassembled the skeleton. Why did the whale die?  The cause was not definitively established. Steve reported shoulder-joint disease and suggested that impaired migration and starvation were possible. Did the whale explode?  Decomposition gases built up in the body, and the carcass ruptured during flensing.

sections.title: 🔬 Science Behind the Story
sections.text: 🔬 Science Behind the Story Flensing:  Removing skin, blubber, and soft tissues from a whale carcass. Decomposition gases:  Microbial breakdown can generate pressure inside a carcass, especially in warm conditions. Bone degreasing:  Whale bones retain substantial oil; prolonged cleaning reduces seepage and deterioration. Osteochondrosis dissecans:  A disorder affecting joint cartilage and underlying bone, potentially limiting joint function. Its role in this whale's death remains a historical interpretation rather than a confirmed cause of death.

sections.title: 🦴 Understanding Osteochondrosis Dissecans (OCD)
sections.text: 🦴 Understanding Osteochondrosis Dissecans (OCD) What is it?  Osteochondrosis is a disorder in which cartilage does not develop into bone normally. Affected joint cartilage can become thickened and weakened. In more advanced lesions, cracks (fissures) can form and a portion of cartilage may partly separate, sometimes involving the bone beneath it. The term  osteochondritis dissecans  is often used for this separating or fragmenting joint lesion. Healthy joint surface OCD: cartilage separation Fissure / flap Smooth articular cartilage Cartilage and underlying bone affected Simplified original teaching diagram, not an image of the Aquarium whale or a veterinary diagnosis. Cartilage is shown in blue; the damaged region is highlighted in red. Why might this matter to a whale?  Damage in a shoulder joint could plausibly reduce comfortable or effective flipper movement. However, how much the condition affected this particular whale is uncertain. What did Steve report?  Steve Webster recalled that a veterinary pathologist identified abnormalities described as osteochondrosis dissecans in the skeleton's shoulder joints. Steve proposed that reduced swimming performance might have interfered with migration and contributed to starvation. That remains his historical interpretation,  not a confirmed cause of death . Terminology note:  Some veterinary pathology references favor the broader term  osteochondrosis , because inflammation is not necessarily present and separation occurs only in some lesions.  Our whale skeleton came from a 26-foot-long, young-of-the-year male gray whale that washed up dead on the beach, right by the Seaside sewage treatment plant at that time, in September. Warm, sunny day. 
 And Julie and our project manager and I went over and sat on the beach and watched this whale washing back and forth in the surf, and asking ourselves, “Do we really want that whale?” 
 And I said, “Well, I know all the students at Moss Landing Marine Lab in the marine mammal class who do dissect whales and get the skeletons out of them. Let's do it.” 
 So we got three tow trucks to pull the whale up out of the beach. Had to wait the next day till two in the afternoon before we could start flensing the whale, because we didn't have a marine mammal permit. In fact, it was illegal just to tow it up the beach. 
 We had to wait for a marine mammal person from the Cal Academy of Sciences to arrive with the permit. So that whale skeleton is on loan, really, from the Cal Academy. 
 Anyway, hot summer September day. As we were waiting for the permit to come, the whale got tighter and tighter and tighter as the gases built up. And so everybody agreed, “Don't anybody cut the body cavity, because this thing's going to explode.” 
 And so we were all working on the rostrum and the flippers and the flukes and the tail, and staying away from the body cavity. Somebody miscalculated. 
 And all of a sudden, boom! This geyser of hot, putrid blood goes about 20 feet in the air. Everybody with these long flensing knives goes dashing off in all directions. Looked like the worst cheap samurai movie you have ever seen. 
 And Julie Packard was there in a white sweatshirt. Why anyone would go to a whale flensing in a white sweatshirt, I don't know. But not one drop of blood touched that sweatshirt. I think Julie has a protective aura around her. 
 So, get the bones out of the whale, bury them in the beach at the Naval Postgraduate School, go back a year later and dig them up, take them to the car wash, convince the man you really want him to let us wash our whale in his car wash. 
 Then you soak the bones in Biz enzyme detergent for about six months. Whale bones are 30 percent oil. You have to get all that oil out, or it starts to rot and drip on your guests. And so, six months. 
 Then firm them up with a very toxic vinylite resin, and then get the guys in the shop to put it all back together in exactly the right arrangement with the advice of Vic Morejohn at Moss Landing Marine Lab. So that's the skeleton that you see out there. 
 And I have one quick story about the skeleton, and then I will let you go. 
 One day, about ten years ago, I got an email from a veterinary pathologist who said, “Do you know that your whale skeleton has osteochondrosis dissecans?” And I thought, I have no idea what that is, and I didn't know our whale had it. 
 It is a degenerative bone disease, and the skeleton has it in the shoulder joints, right below the shoulder blades there. 
 So I grabbed our veterinarian, Mike Murray, and walked him out there, and I said, “Mike, look at the shoulder joints. What do you see?” “Ah, osteochondrosis dissecans.” 
 So that explains why that whale didn't make the migration, probably starved to death and washed up dead on the beach. There had been no apparent net damage or any other trauma.

sections.title: 📖 Steve Webster's Story
sections.text: 📖 Steve Webster's Story A 26-foot-long, young-of-the-year male gray whale washed ashore near the Seaside sewage treatment plant. Steve Webster and colleagues decided to recover its skeleton. Three tow trucks were brought in to move the whale, but the team had to wait for a marine mammal permit before flensing could begin. In the September warmth, decomposition gases built up inside the carcass. The team warned everyone to avoid cutting the body cavity, but someone miscalculated. The carcass ruptured, sending a geyser of hot, putrid blood about 20 feet into the air. People holding long flensing knives scattered. Steve compared the scene to a cheap samurai movie. Julie Packard was present wearing a white sweatshirt; astonishingly, not a drop of blood touched it. The bones were buried on the beach at the Naval Postgraduate School, recovered about a year later, cleaned at a car wash, and soaked in Biz enzyme detergent for approximately six months to remove oil. The bones were then stabilized with vinylite resin and reassembled with advice from Vic Morejohn of Moss Landing Marine Laboratories. Years later, a veterinary pathologist noticed osteochondrosis dissecans in the shoulder joints. Steve suggested the condition may have interfered with the whale's migration and contributed to starvation. No obvious net damage or other trauma had been found.

sections.title: ❓ Visitor Questions
sections.text: ❓ Visitor Questions What whale is this?  A young-of-the-year male gray whale, about 26 feet long. Where was it found?  On the beach near the Seaside sewage treatment plant. How did the Aquarium prepare the skeleton?  The team recovered and flensed the carcass, buried the bones for about a year, cleaned and degreased them, stabilized them with resin, and reassembled the skeleton. Why did the whale die?  The cause was not definitively established. Steve reported shoulder-joint disease and suggested that impaired migration and starvation were possible. Did the whale explode?  Decomposition gases built up in the body, and the carcass ruptured during flensing.

sections.title: 🔬 Science Behind the Story
sections.text: 🔬 Science Behind the Story Flensing:  Removing skin, blubber, and soft tissues from a whale carcass. Decomposition gases:  Microbial breakdown can generate pressure inside a carcass, especially in warm conditions. Bone degreasing:  Whale bones retain substantial oil; prolonged cleaning reduces seepage and deterioration. Osteochondrosis dissecans:  A disorder affecting joint cartilage and underlying bone, potentially limiting joint function. Its role in this whale's death remains a historical interpretation rather than a confirmed cause of death.

sections.title: 🦴 Understanding Osteochondrosis Dissecans (OCD)
sections.text: 🦴 Understanding Osteochondrosis Dissecans (OCD) What is it?  Osteochondrosis is a disorder in which cartilage does not develop into bone normally. Affected joint cartilage can become thickened and weakened. In more advanced lesions, cracks (fissures) can form and a portion of cartilage may partly separate, sometimes involving the bone beneath it. The term  osteochondritis dissecans  is often used for this separating or fragmenting joint lesion. Healthy joint surface OCD: cartilage separation Fissure / flap Smooth articular cartilage Cartilage and underlying bone affected Simplified original teaching diagram, not an image of the Aquarium whale or a veterinary diagnosis. Cartilage is shown in blue; the damaged region is highlighted in red. Why might this matter to a whale?  Damage in a shoulder joint could plausibly reduce comfortable or effective flipper movement. However, how much the condition affected this particular whale is uncertain. What did Steve report?  Steve Webster recalled that a veterinary pathologist identified abnormalities described as osteochondrosis dissecans in the skeleton's shoulder joints. Steve proposed that reduced swimming performance might have interfered with migration and contributed to starvation. That remains his historical interpretation,  not a confirmed cause of death . Terminology note:  Some veterinary pathology references favor the broader term  osteochondrosis , because inflammation is not necessarily present and separation occurs only in some lesions. Further reading:  NIH/NTP Nonneoplastic Lesion Atlas: Osteochondrosis ↗  ·  NIH GARD: Osteochondritis dissecans ↗ . General pathology sources, not case-specific examination reports.

sections.title: 1. What is a falsejingle?
sections.text: 1. What is a falsejingle? A slender bivalve that is sometimes called a rock oyster, although it is not an oyster. Falsejingles are cementing bivalves: rather than remaining mobile as adults, they permanently attach to a surface.

sections.title: 2. Life Cycle & Settlement
sections.text: 2. Life Cycle & Settlement Like other bivalves, falsejingles pass through free-swimming larval stages. In the pediveliger stage the larva has a small muscular foot. The source Field Note describes final settlement using a byssus plug made from a composite of proteins and calcium carbonate. The plug passes through the opening in the lower shell and hardens into a permanent anchor.

sections.title: 3. Filter Feeding & Water Quality
sections.text: 3. Filter Feeding & Water Quality Falsejingles filter water for plankton and suspended nutrients. As with other bivalves, this can remove particulates and excess nutrients and improve water clarity. Bivalves can also accumulate some metals and contaminants, which is why they can be useful indicators of environmental conditions.

sections.title: 4. Ecosystem Services
sections.text: 4. Ecosystem Services Although falsejingles do not build dense reefs like mussels or oysters, their shells add hard surfaces used by barnacles, bryozoans, feather-duster worms, coralline algae and other encrusting organisms. Their filtering also links them to nutrient cycling and water clarity.

sections.title: 5. Predators & Food Web
sections.text: 5. Predators & Food Web Predators listed in the source include sunflower, ochre, mottled and rainbow stars, giant Pacific octopus and black oystercatchers. A cited Alaska octopus study found falsejingles among commonly consumed bivalves in some giant Pacific octopus middens, illustrating that individuals can specialize even within a generally broad diet.

sections.title: 6. Where to Look at the Aquarium
sections.text: 6. Where to Look at the Aquarium The source note says there is no dedicated falsejingle exhibit. They can be found by looking carefully in Monterey Bay Habitats, including along the ledge of the large Monterey Bay Habitats exhibit and on hard surfaces in several exhibits.

sections.title: 7. Guide Talking Points
sections.text: 7. Guide Talking Points “Mermaid’s toenails” is a memorable common name for an easily overlooked bivalve. Unlike a burrowing clam, the adult permanently cements itself to hard substrate. Its shell becomes habitat for other organisms. Filter feeding connects a small animal to water clarity, nutrient cycling and the larger food web.

sections.title: Quick guide
sections.text: Quick guide Hopkins’ rose is a vividly pink dorid nudibranch, often seen on rocky shores of the California coast. Its northward appearances during unusually warm ocean periods make it a useful species for discussing changing marine conditions. Size:  2–3 cm •  Food:  red bryozoans •  Habitat:  rocky intertidal •  Scientific name:   Ceratodoris rosacea .

sections.title: Life cycle and pink eggs
sections.text: Life cycle and pink eggs Pink egg ribbons hatch into swimming veliger larvae, which settle and metamorphose into shell-less juveniles. Adults are hermaphrodites. Egg masses — iNaturalist. Life cycle — Zoe Lawrence.

sections.title: Dorid versus aeolid
sections.text: Dorid versus aeolid Although its papillae resemble aeolid cerata, Hopkins’ rose is a dorid with branchial gills near its anus. The gills can be hidden among papillae. Comparison — Kitty Turner. Important correction: this image incorrectly labels Hopkins’ rose as an aeolid. Branchial gills — Robin Agarwal.

sections.title: Rhinophores and camouflage
sections.text: Rhinophores and camouflage Rhinophores are sensory structures that detect chemical cues. They can be difficult to spot among the long papillae. Rhinophores — Jerry Kirkhart. Pale animal showing gills and rhinophores — iNaturalist.

sections.title: Pink coloration and diet
sections.text: Pink coloration and diet Prey-derived pigments, including hopkinsiaxanthin, contribute to the vivid pink color. Bright coloration can serve as a warning to predators. Color intensity alone does not establish health.

sections.title: Warm-water range shifts
sections.text: Warm-water range shifts Warm-water episodes, including the 2015–16 El Niño and marine heatwave, coincided with unusual sightings far north of the species’ usual Southern California range.

sections.title: In 30 seconds
sections.text: Concepts · Guide reference In 30 seconds iNaturalist  is an international biodiversity observation platform. People share photos or sounds of wild organisms, and community members help identify them. Some observations support scientific research. For Aquarium guides:  a sighting can spark a great conversation, but a reported identification is not always confirmed. We share the interesting takeaway first and link to the original observation for anyone who wants to explore further.

sections.title: What is iNaturalist, and is it credible?
sections.text: What is iNaturalist, and is it credible? iNaturalist began as a UC Berkeley student project, later became a joint initiative of the California Academy of Sciences and National Geographic Society, and became an independent nonprofit in 2023. It is a serious international citizen-science platform—not just a local enthusiasts' club. Contributors include interested members of the public, experienced naturalists, taxonomists and professional scientists. The platform is not itself a government regulator or the final authority on accepted taxonomy. iNaturalist: About ↗

sections.title: How reliable is a sighting?
sections.text: How reliable is a sighting? Observations can be labeled  Casual ,  Needs ID , or  Research Grade . Research Grade means applicable evidence, data-quality and community-identification criteria were met. It does  not  mean a professional expert necessarily verified the organism, or that an identification cannot change. A single unusual sighting does not establish a species' population size, rarity or a change in its geographic range. When identification is uncertain, we say so. iNaturalist Help Center ↗

sections.title: Do scientists use these observations?
sections.text: Do scientists use these observations? Yes. Eligible iNaturalist observations are shared with biodiversity data systems such as the  Global Biodiversity Information Facility (GBIF)  and can help researchers study where organisms occur. Scientific conclusions still require appropriate checks and context.

sections.title: How do we use iNaturalist in MBA Hub?
sections.text: How do we use iNaturalist in MBA Hub? Our priority is the Aquarium guest experience.  We select observations that are interesting or useful to guides, write a short visitor-friendly takeaway, and—when available—link to the exact original observation. Keep it compact:  a brief note or Species Highlight, not a large photo gallery or database. Distinguish sources:  MJ's firsthand sightings, other people's reports, and published scientific findings are different kinds of evidence. Respect uncertainty:  use “reported,” “possibly,” or “identification uncertain” where appropriate. Respect creators:  link to the original observation rather than copying photographs without checking permission or license. Avoid duplication:  dated sightings stay in Naturalist Field Notes; enduring animal information belongs in Species Guides. This Concepts app explains the source and our standards. Unusual sightings do not automatically require new standalone Species Guides. We add one only when it has lasting Aquarium interpretive value.

sections.title: For curious guides: evidence and scientific authority
sections.text: For curious guides: evidence and scientific authority Use scientific studies and appropriate taxonomic references for broader conclusions and current accepted species names. Use established monitoring programs for population trends. iNaturalist is especially useful for documented individual sightings; its observation counts are not a population census. Three layers of depth:  (1) guide essentials, visible immediately; (2) optional biology and context; (3) original records and scientific sources, available when needed.

sections.title: RELATE
sections.text: relate RELATE Start with visitors' reactions Begin with what guests see, feel, notice, and wonder — not with what the volunteer wants to teach first. Interpretation begins with the visitor's own reaction. This validates curiosity and helps visitors feel immediately connected to the exhibit. Try saying What drew your eye first? That's a great observation — I noticed that too! What does this remind you of? Notice first, teach second. visitor engagement questions observations conversation starter

sections.title: REVEAL
sections.text: reveal REVEAL Connect info to the visitor's reaction — bring the wow Connect information to what the guest already noticed so the meaning lands. Instead of giving random facts, connect information to the guest's initial reaction. This is where the aha moment happens. Example exchange Visitor The kelp looks like it's dancing. Volunteer It really does! Those waves aren't just pretty — they help the kelp get the nutrients it needs. Tie the fact to the visitor's observation. aha moment kelp forest meaning facts

sections.title: STORIES
sections.text: stories STORIES Inform, entertain, and enlighten Use stories, comparisons, and memorable images so visitors care and remember. Stories are how humans make meaning. They create emotional connections and help guests remember what they learned. Interpretation is an art — use it. Examples Giant kelp can grow two feet a day. Imagine if your houseplants did that! Sea otters are like the forest keepers — they protect the kelp by eating urchins. Make the idea memorable. storytelling sea otters kelp forest memory metaphor

sections.title: ENGAGE
sections.text: engage ENGAGE Ask questions as well as answer them Invite visitors into the conversation so they think, notice, and participate. Interpretation should provoke curiosity, not just deliver information. Guests think more deeply when invited into the conversation. Examples Why do you think the fish school that way? What do you notice about how the kelp moves? Which animals draw your attention? Turn facts into conversation. questions visitor engagement fish conversation

sections.title: WHOLE
sections.text: whole WHOLE Present a whole rather than a part Help guests see systems, relationships, and the full picture rather than isolated facts. Help guests see the full picture — connections, systems, relationships — rather than isolated facts. This deepens understanding and sparks wonder about how everything fits together. Examples What you're seeing here is a whole forest under water: animals, plants, water movement, light — they all depend on each other. Every species in the kelp forest helps keep the ecosystem in balance. If one suddenly went away, the entire forest would be affected. Connect the parts into a system. ecosystem kelp forest systems connections balance

sections.title: ADJUST
sections.text: adjust ADJUST Children need a different approach, not a simplified adult one Use imagination, motion, metaphor, and feelings when speaking with children. Kids are not adults with fewer facts. They interpret the world through touch, metaphor, emotion, and imagination. Different approaches help them connect authentically. For children What does this fish remind you of? Can you move your hand like the kelp sways? How do you feel looking at the animals in the kelp forest? Change the approach, not just the vocabulary. kids families movement emotion imagination

sections.title: Kelp Forest
sections.text:
Kelp Forest Exhibits EXHIBIT EXHIBIT_SPACE 1.2.3 2026-06-26 Guide-friendly companion page for the Monterey Bay Aquarium Kelp Forest exhibit, with quick facts, visitor Q&A, conservation messages, volunteer talking points, references, and troubleshooting support. Core update This version adds an easy close button to the Troubleshooting panel while preserving the top-bar controls. View into a kelp forest exhibit with kelp and fish MBA Naturalist Library image approved for internal volunteer Hub use. ~400 individual fish on exhibit, not counting schooling anchovies. About 42 fish species, 56 invertebrate species, and 67 algae species are represented in the exhibit census. The exhibit is about 31 feet deep total, with about 28 feet of water. The exhibit holds approximately 340,000 gallons, or about 1.26 million liters, of seawater. Water enters at about 1,600 gallons per minute, with a full turnover about every 2 to 2.5 hours. Typical exhibit temperature range: 48–58°F, or about 8.9–14.4°C. Kelp in the exhibit is commonly reported to grow about 4–5 inches per day. Feeding is usually once daily, often around 11:30 a.m. or 2:30 p.m.; exact timing can vary. Giant kelp can grow several inches in a single day. It makes an underwater forest where fish can hide, hunt, rest, and grow up. Look into the Kelp Forest and imagine swimming through a forest where the trees sway with the waves instead of the wind. Giant kelp forms the living structure, while fish, crabs, sea stars, anemones, urchins, and many other animals use different parts of the forest like rooms in a home.

This exhibit is one of the Aquarium’s signature achievements. Before the Aquarium opened in 1984, growing giant kelp successfully in an aquarium had not been done at this scale. The open top brings in sunlight, cold bay water brings nutrients, and the surge machine creates the back-and-forth motion kelp needs.

A good visitor message is simple: kelp forests are communities. When we protect the habitat, make smart seafood choices, and support healthy ocean management, the whole community has a better chance to thrive. Exhibit dimensions and systems The Kelp Forest exhibit is approximately 66 feet long by 28 feet wide, with a total depth of about 31 feet and about 28 feet of water. It holds approximately 340,000 gallons of seawater. Water turnover is commonly listed at about 1,600 gallons per minute, with a full turnover about every 2 to 2.5 hours. The first-floor windows are about 15 feet tall and 7.25 inches thick, weighing about 2.5 tons each. The rockwork is fiberglass-reinforced concrete, not real rock. How the kelp stays alive The exhibit is open to the sky so giant kelp can receive direct sunlight for photosynthesis. Cold, nutrient-rich seawater from Monterey Bay helps support kelp growth. A surge machine built into the left rockwork creates a standing wave, often described as about 12–14 inches, to mimic natural ocean surge and keep nutrients moving across the kelp. Animals on exhibit Commonly noted animals include northern anchovies, blue rockfish, blacksmith, gopher rockfish, striped seaperch, señorita, kelp surfperch, salema, halfmoon, opaleye, red sea urchin, copper rockfish, giant kelpfish, black rockfish, California sea cucumber, northern kelp crab, kelp greenling, California sheephead, kelp bass, bat stars, leopard sharks, wolf eels, giant sea bass, swell shark, and spiny lobster. Counts change over time, so use the current animal census for precise daily numbers. Fish ecology Kelp forests create many living spaces: canopy, midwater, rock faces, crevices, holdfasts, and the seafloor. Small schooling fish may use the forest as shelter. Rockfish, surfperch, kelpfish, and other species use the structure in different ways. Predators such as kelp bass, giant sea bass, leopard sharks, wolf eels, and larger rockfish help shape the community. Invertebrates and algae Invertebrates are a major part of the kelp forest community. Sea stars, anemones, crabs, sea cucumbers, urchins, chitons, limpets, and spiny lobsters all use the habitat. Some filter food from the water, some graze algae, some eat drifting kelp pieces, and some hunt or scavenge. Giant kelp, Macrocystis pyrifera, is the ecosystem engineer that creates much of the structure. Conservation messaging Kelp forests connect naturally to three visitor messages: protect habitat, choose seafood responsibly, and understand the value of marine protected areas. Rockfish recovery is a strong local story: many rockfish populations were hurt by overfishing, and better management helped many groundfish fisheries improve. Marine protected areas can work like a bank account for ocean life, allowing animals and habitats to recover and support surrounding waters. Spanish naming note The exhibit name in Spanish is Bosque de Macroalgas. The Spanish common name note from the source app says giant kelp should be referred to as macrocistis rather than the outdated cachiyuyo. Use current MBA Naturalist Library language standards when updating this page. How deep is the Kelp Forest tank? It is about 31 feet deep total, with about 28 feet of water. The first-floor windows are about 15 feet tall and over 7 inches thick. How much water does it hold? About 340,000 gallons, or roughly 1.26 million liters. Water is pumped in from Monterey Bay and turns over about every 2 to 2.5 hours. Are the rocks real? No. The rockwork is fiberglass-reinforced concrete. It is designed to look like natural rocky reef while staying strong and lightweight enough for the exhibit. How fast does kelp grow? In this exhibit, kelp is commonly reported to grow about 4–5 inches per day. Growth depends on light, nutrients, water motion, and conditions in the exhibit. Why is the exhibit open at the top? Giant kelp needs sunlight for photosynthesis, so the open top lets natural light reach the kelp. That is one of the features that helps this living forest grow indoors. What makes the wave? A surge machine built into the rockwork pushes water back and forth. That motion mimics natural ocean surge and helps move nutrients across the kelp. When is feeding? Feeding is usually once daily, often around 11:30 a.m. or 2:30 p.m., but times can vary. Check the day’s schedule before giving visitors a specific time. What do the animals eat? The exhibit diet may include items such as squid, shrimp or prawns, whitefish, sardines, and krill. Different animals feed in different ways, just as they would in a natural kelp forest food web. What is an MPA? An MPA is a Marine Protected Area. It is a place where some activities are limited so ocean life and habitats have room to recover and grow. Why are kelp forests important? They provide food, shelter, nursery space, and hunting grounds for many animals. They also help visitors see that a habitat is more than a backdrop — it is a living community. Start with what visitors can see: swaying kelp, schooling fish, rockfish holding still, sea stars on the windows, or the surge moving the whole forest. Helpful analogy: kelp is like the trees in a forest, but it is algae, not a plant. It creates structure that many animals use. Another analogy: MPAs can work like a bank account for ocean health — life grows inside and can help surrounding waters over time. Point out that the rocks are not real. This often surprises visitors and opens a conversation about exhibit design. For kids, invite them to look for camouflage: giant kelpfish can blend into kelp, while rockfish often hover near structure. For conservation, connect kelp forests to Seafood Watch: responsible seafood choices help people and ocean wildlife share healthy food webs. Common misunderstanding: kelp is not a tree and not a true plant. Giant kelp is a brown alga. sections.title: 🐋 Blue Whale Ear Bone
sections.text: blue-whale-ear-bone 🐋 Blue Whale Ear Bone Marine Mammal Cart Blue whale hearing, songs, migration, krill feeding, and Monterey Bay connections. Male blue whales are the loudest animals on the planet! Their calls to find females can be heard up to 1,000 miles away. Their survival literally depends on their ability to hear one another. However, the ocean is becoming an increasingly noisy place, mostly due to shipping noise. Luckily, our bay and the surrounding waters are part of a sanctuary, so commercial vessels give the area a wide berth to reduce underwater noise pollution. Simple steps like this will help blue whale populations continue to grow. Currently, the North Eastern Pacific population is around 2,000 blue whales. The blue whales that visit Monterey Bay spend their winters in warm tropical waters near Costa Rica where pregnant mothers give birth to their calves. But, there's not much to eat there. Each spring, they migrate thousands of miles to feast in the nutrient-rich waters of Monterey Bay, where krill, a tiny shrimp-like animal, occurs in huge swarms during most springs and summers. A single blue whale can eat more than 5,000 pounds of krill every day. Specimen label: Blue whale ear bone English: Blue whales can hear one another's calls a thousand miles apart. Discussion prompt: Why do blue whales visit Monterey Bay? English: Blue whales migrate thousands of miles to strain krill from the bay. sections.text: dolphin-jaw 🐬 Dolphin Jaw Marine Mammal Cart Dolphin hearing, echolocation, teamwork, prey herding, and Monterey Bay visits. Dolphins like these have a great trick up their sleeve to help find and catch prey. They send out a series of high-pitched clicks, which bounce off their prey and back to their jaw, not their ear. This sound-based locating strategy means they can find food in water that has poor visibility, or even in the dark! Pacific white-sided dolphins that visit Monterey Bay don't stay year-round. They roam the west coast of the United States in search of fish and squid. When the pod discovers a school of prey, they work together cooperatively to herd the school into a tight ball, making the fish easier to catch. Specimen label: Dolphin jaw English: Dolphins hear with help from their jawbones. Spanish: Los delfines oyen con la ayuda de sus mandíbulas. sections.title: 🐳 Orca Tooth
sections.text: orca-tooth 🐳 Orca Tooth Marine Mammal Cart Orca teeth, salmon, gray whale migration, top predator behavior, and Monterey Bay prey. Some orcas live year-round in the waters of the Pacific Northwest. They specialize in eating fish, especially salmon. They travel south when food is scarce in their home waters, and visit our bay in search of food. Once they've found a school of salmon, orcas use clicks and whistles to communicate and coordinate with other members of the pod. Their remarkable combination of size, speed, and exceptional senses are some of the reasons why orcas are the top of the ocean food web. Each year, gray whale families pass through Monterey during long migrations between Alaska and Mexico. Some orcas specialize in eating marine mammals, including gray whales. During the peak of the gray whale's northward migration through our bay, orcas visit in search of younger, more vulnerable grays. But because Monterey Bay sees lots of marine mammals, orcas may visit year-round in search of prey. Specimen label: Orca tooth English: Orcas use their teeth to grasp and tear prey. sections.title: 🦭 Elephant Seal Flipper
sections.text: elephant-seal-flipper 🦭 Elephant Seal Flipper Marine Mammal Cart Elephant seal flippers, recovery from near extinction, bull males, harems, and California colonies. The elephant seal's recovery from near extinction is a testament to the effectiveness of protection. Elephant seals were once hunted nearly to extinction; their blubber was used for making lamp oil. 100 years ago, there were less than 100 seals remaining. Today, large colonies of elephant seals can be found just to the north and south of Monterey Bay. Over 200,000 elephant seals call California home. Scientists consider the population healthy and robust. Large bulls, weighing up to 5,000 pounds, protect their harem of females from rival males. A successful bull can have a harem of up to 100 females! Smaller males have no chance of finding a mate, so they steer clear of beaches where larger males are already established. They can sometimes be found on local beaches, hoping that a stray female will find his territory attractive. Specimen label: Elephant seal front flipper English: An elephant seal's front flippers have five digits, like a human hand. Spanish: Alguna vez cazadas casi hasta su extinción, hoy en día el número de focas elefante supera los 160,000. Discussion prompt: Why is bigger better for male elephant seals? sections.title: 🦦 Sea Otter Skull
sections.text: sea-otter-skull 🦦 Sea Otter Skull Marine Mammal Cart Sea otter skull, jaws, kelp forests, urchins, tools, armpit pockets, and predator role. Otters are a top predator of urchins in our kelp forests. Urchins are herbivores who eat kelp. If they become too abundant, they can literally make a kelp forest disappear, leaving what's known as an 'urchin barren' in their wake. That's where otters come in — they eat the urchins that eat the kelp! When otters, urchins, and kelp are in balance, we have healthy kelp forests that support an entire community of algae and animals. Otters often place a rock on their chest to help open hard-shelled prey — they bang the prey against the hard surface to crack it open and get to the tasty meat inside. They might keep their favorite rock stashed in an armpit pocket! Otters also use tools while underwater; brute strength is not enough to pry an abalone loose, so the otter uses a stone as a chisel. Otters are one of the few mammals that use tools on a daily basis. But not all food requires a tool: southern sea otters eat invertebrates, not fish, so many of their prey items are soft and squishy! Specimen label: Sea otter skull English: Strong jaws and teeth help make sea otters top predators. Spanish: Poderosas mandíbulas y dientes permiten que las nutrias marinas sean consideradas un animal superdepredador. Discussion prompt: How do sea otters help kelp forests? English: Sea otters keep sea urchin populations in check so kelp forests can thrive. Spanish: Las nutrias marinas mantienen bajo control a las poblaciones de erizos de mar para que los bosques de cachiyuyo puedan prosperar. Discussion prompt: What does a sea otter hide in its pockets? English: Sea otters stash rocks in folds of fur under their arms so they can crack open food. sections.title: 🐋 Humpback Whale Food
sections.text: humpback-whale-food 🐋 Humpback Whale Food Marine Mammal Cart Humpback whale food, Monterey Bay feeding, migration, schooling fish, and bubble-net feeding. Humpbacks visit our bay each spring and summer for the same reason that people have fished here for thousands of years. These humpbacks spend their winters in the warm waters of Costa Rica, but travel thousands of miles to feast in Monterey Bay. Even mothers with newborn calves make the journey! But the trip is worth it — our rich waters provide an all-you-can-eat buffet. Humpbacks in Alaska work as a team when hunting for schooling fish. Once underwater, several of the humpbacks encircle the fish with a 'bubble net', which the fish won't cross. Other whales position themselves below the school and swim upward to force the fish toward the surface. The whole group of humpbacks will lunge up through the concentrated school of fish, feasting on thousands of fish in a single mouthful. Specimen label: Humpback whale food English: Both humans and humpbacks enjoy Monterey Bay's bountiful feast. Spanish: Tanto los humanos como los rorcuales jorobados disfrutan de los abundantes manjares de la Bahía de Monterey. Discussion prompt: Why do humpbacks travel to Monterey Bay? Spanish: Los rorcuales jorobados migran miles de millas para alimentarse de los cardúmenes de peces que hay en la bahía. Discussion prompt: Why do humpbacks blow bubbles under water? English: Humpbacks work as a team by encircling fish in a bubble net and lunging from below. Spanish: Los rorcuales funcionan como equipo. sections.text: 2026-01-15-gray-whale-migration-ecology-conservation January 15, 2026 (Bay Watch January 8–14) Gray Whales: Migration, Feeding, Calves & Conservation Gray whale calves nurse on exceptionally rich milk and grow rapidly before migrating north with their mothers. Gray whales disturb seafloor sediment while feeding and can influence benthic food webs; Arctic sea ice and prey availability may influence survival. The 2018–2023 eastern North Pacific gray whale unusual mortality event was associated with malnutrition and reduced reproductive success; exact causal contributions remain under study. Migration and seasonal sightings Growth, calves and reproduction The source describes gestation of about 12–13 months, calves roughly 14–15 ft at birth, rich milk and rapid growth, weaning around 6–7 months, and maturity generally years later. Adult breeding groups may include a female and multiple males, and courtship can occur during migration. The source gives illustrative estimates of calf milk intake and adult seasonal weight loss; figures vary across studies. Barnacles, whale lice and feeding-side preference Ecosystem engineers and flexible diets Bottom feeding creates sediment disturbances and feeding pits, redistributing sediment and potentially making prey available to seabirds. Gray whales feed heavily on benthic amphipods but also use other prey and habitats, including mysids, krill and other invertebrates; some unusual fish-feeding observations are reported. Sea-ice algae can support Arctic benthic food webs, but feeding ecology and changes in prey are complex. Population declines, UME and conservation The author highlights a large decline from a roughly 2016 population estimate near 27,000 to more recent estimates near 13,000, and a reported very low calf count of 85 in the previous season. The NOAA-designated 2018–2023 unusual mortality event involved hundreds of documented strandings across Mexico, the United States and Canada; malnutrition and changing prey availability are leading concerns, with vessel strikes and entanglement additional threats. Do not present one unproven cause as settled, and distinguish monitoring counts from abundance estimates. Eastern and western North Pacific populations have different conservation contexts; the Pacific Coast Feeding Group is a distinct feeding aggregation within the eastern population. sections.text: 2026-03-12-pacific-white-sided-dolphin ../../shared/media/asset-dbfeba5da571feb6--IMG_3509.jpeg Pacific white-sided dolphin, standard coloration Pacific white-sided dolphin — standard coloration (title illustration). March 12, 2026 (Bay Watch March 5–11) Pacific White-Sided Dolphins • Brownell Morph • Mixed-Species Superpods Species Highlight: Pacific white-sided dolphin, including the uncommon Brownell color morph and 2025 proposed taxonomic changes. Social behavior, regional stock, reproduction, diving-depth uncertainty and mixed-species superpods. Bay Watch March 5–11, 2026, including gray whale mating groups, CA200 orcas, red phalaropes and salmon shark. Pacific white-sided dolphins — standard and Brownell color morphs Pacific white-sided dolphins visit Monterey Bay year-round and may occur with northbound mating gray whales in spring. A recurring Brownell color morph shows a contrasting pale outline and darker side patch. The author compares its appearance with hourglass dolphins. ../../shared/media/asset-922d38f86c89f73d--IMG_3505.jpeg Illustrated comparison: standard Pacific white-sided dolphin coloration (top) and Brownell morph (bottom). Source-provided image. ../../shared/media/asset-a547e5af9334e5b1--IMG_3506.jpeg Photographs of standard morph (left) and Brownell morph (right). Source-provided image. 2025 proposed dolphin reclassification The source's 2025 illustration proposes Aethalodelphis obliquidens for Pacific white-sided dolphins, alongside Aethalodelphis obscurus for dusky dolphins, while retaining other species in Leucopleurus, Lagenorhynchus and Cephalorhynchus. This is presented as the supplied proposed taxonomic treatment; nomenclature may vary by authority. ../../shared/media/asset-07e9859dce7506c6--IMG_3507.jpeg 2025 proposed reclassification chart, credited on the image to Uko Gorter; references include Galatius et al. (2025). Habitat, regional stock and diving uncertainty The author reports North Pacific distribution from Mexico to China and north to Alaska and Russia; nearshore and offshore habitats; prey of schooling fishes and squid; orcas as predators. The California–Oregon–Washington stock is described as roughly 21,000–35,000 dolphins and stable. Photo identification suggests pods return to Monterey Bay, though smaller-scale site fidelity remains insufficiently studied. Some sources claim dives to 3,280 ft, but the author questions this in view of reported six-minute dives and proposes nocturnal vertical prey migration as an alternative; the proposed 600–1,000 ft depth is speculation, not a measured limit. Reproduction and social life The source describes mating behaviors especially in late summer and fall; gestation 9–12 months; calves averaging 3 ft and 30 lb; weaning generally near 12 months and sometimes 18 months; births every 2–5 years; female maturity around 8–10 years and male maturity around 10–11 years. Social structure and natal pod retention are not well studied; the author's suggested connection between non-menopause and weaker multigenerational pods is an inference. Mixed-species groups and superpods Pacific white-sided dolphins often associate with northern right whale dolphins and sometimes Risso’s dolphins, sea lions or baleen whales. Predator avoidance, foraging, mating and social behavior are suggested explanations for mixed-species groups and temporary superpods exceeding 1,000 animals; these remain hypotheses. The author commonly sees groups of around 15–20 and reports Pacific white-sided dolphins as frequent participants in Monterey Bay superpods, often alongside northern right whale dolphins. ../../shared/media/asset-81892438cc2e6a55--IMG_3508.jpeg Pacific white-sided dolphin Lagenorhynchus obliquidens (proposed 2025: Aethalodelphis obliquidens) ../pacific-white-sided-dolphin/index.html A highly social North Pacific dolphin with standard and Brownell coloration, frequent Monterey Bay visits, and spectacular mixed-species superpods. Length: 5.5–8 ft; average around 7 ft (source figures). Weight: 175–440 lb; typical 300–400 lb (source figures). Diet: schooling fish and squid, including anchovies, sardines, herring, whiting and market squid. Predators: orcas; habitat: nearshore and offshore North Pacific. Lifespan: approximately 36–42 years on average, maximum reported 46 years. Conservation status: Least Concern (as reported in source). California–Oregon–Washington stock estimated at 21,000–35,000 in source; current estimate not independently checked. Diving depths of 3,280 ft are questioned by the author; do not present them as verified. Brownell morph is a recurring coloration pattern, not albinism. sections.title: May 20, 2026 (Bay Watch May 14–20) — Marine Mammal Cart Narrations • Hopkins’ Rose Nudibranch • Sea Slug Search
sections.text: 2026-05-20-hopkins-rose-marine-mammal-cart May 20, 2026 (Bay Watch May 14–20) Marine Mammal Cart Narrations • Hopkins’ Rose Nudibranch • Sea Slug Search Marine Mammal Cart training and six prop narration guides with expandable visitor questions. Species Highlight: Hopkins’ rose nudibranch (Ceratodoris rosacea), seven illustrated images. Sea Slug Search 2026; Bay Watch May 14–20, 2026. Marine Mammal Cart — prop-by-prop narration guide Select a prop to open its suggested visitor questions and interpretive talking points. The accompanying handout also provides Spanish wording. The guide below paraphrases the source; videos on the physical cart are not embedded. Blue whale ear bone Blue whales hear calls across immense distances. Why do male blue whales sing? Male blue whales sing to find females over vast distances. Their low-frequency calls can travel up to 1,000 miles. Underwater noise from shipping can interfere with communication. Why do blue whales visit Monterey Bay? They migrate thousands of miles from warm breeding waters to Monterey Bay to feed on dense krill swarms. An individual may eat thousands of pounds of krill daily. El hueso del oído de la ballena azul. Las ballenas azules pueden oír los llamados de otras a mil millas de distancia. Dolphin jaw Dolphins receive sound vibrations through their lower jaws. How do dolphins find food in dark waters? Dolphins emit high-pitched echolocation clicks; returning echoes travel through the lower jaw to the auditory system, allowing them to locate prey in poor visibility. How does teamwork help dolphins catch prey? Pacific white-sided dolphins cooperate to herd schools of fish into dense bait balls, making prey easier to capture. La mandíbula del delfín. Los delfines oyen con la ayuda de sus mandíbulas. Orca tooth Orcas grasp and tear prey with strong teeth. Why do Pacific Northwest orcas visit Monterey Bay? Some fish-eating orcas travel in search of prey when food is scarce. Different orca populations have different prey preferences; do not assume all local orcas eat salmon. What whales do orcas hunt in Monterey Bay? Some mammal-eating orcas hunt gray whales, especially vulnerable calves during their northward migration; orcas also pursue other marine mammals. El diente de una orca. Las orcas usan sus dientes para sujetar y despedazar a su presa. Elephant seal front flipper Elephant seal front flippers have five digits, like a human hand. How many northern elephant seals live in California? Once nearly hunted to extinction for their oil, northern elephant seals rebounded following protections. The source handout cites more than 160,000 in one section and more than 200,000 in another; treat these as differing estimates, not one confirmed count. Why is bigger better for male elephant seals? Large bulls can defend breeding territories and mate with many females; smaller males are often excluded by dominant bulls. La aleta delantera de la foca elefante. Tienen cinco dígitos similares a los de una mano humana. Sea otter skull Powerful jaws and teeth help sea otters crush hard-shelled prey. How do sea otters help kelp forests? Sea otters eat sea urchins. By limiting urchin grazing, they help maintain kelp forests and the many species these forests support. What do sea otters keep in their pockets? Loose folds of skin beneath the forelimbs can hold food or favorite stones. Sea otters use rocks to break open shellfish. Cráneo de nutria marina. Poderosas mandíbulas y dientes permiten que las nutrias marinas sean superdepredadores. Humpback whale food Monterey Bay provides abundant prey for visiting humpbacks. Why do humpbacks travel to Monterey Bay? Humpbacks migrate from warmer breeding grounds to productive feeding areas, where they eat schooling fish and other prey. Why do humpbacks blow bubbles underwater? Some humpbacks, especially in Alaska, cooperate in bubble-net feeding: bubbles concentrate schooling fish and whales lunge upward to capture them. Alimento del rorcual jorobado. La Bahía de Monterey ofrece abundante alimento. Sea Slug Search 2026 — volunteer opportunity The author is volunteering Friday morning with the Pacific Grove Museum of Natural History for Sea Slug Search 2026, hosted by the California Academy of Sciences on iNaturalist. A recent survey at Asilomar found dozens of nudibranchs spanning more than a dozen species. The event announcement is preserved as originally described, not presented as a current upcoming event. Hopkins’ rose — eggs and nudibranch life cycle Hopkins’ rose lays pink egg masses. The source describes a typical nudibranch life cycle: eggs hatch into swimming veliger larvae; larvae settle, lose their larval shells and develop into benthic juveniles before reaching reproductive maturity. Nudibranchs are simultaneous hermaphrodites. Species-specific development has not been well studied under human care. ../../shared/media/asset-538d5993b59b2206--IMG_3465.jpeg Hopkins’ rose nudibranchs and their pink egg ribbon — iNaturalist. ../../shared/media/asset-717b2911c7edcb80--IMG_3466.jpeg Nudibranch life cycle — Zoe Lawrence. Hopkins’ rose — dorid, not aeolid Despite its many long papillae, Hopkins’ rose is a dorid nudibranch, not an aeolid. Dorids possess a branchial plume of gills near the anus, whereas aeolids have dorsal cerata. The gill plumes and sensory rhinophores of Hopkins’ rose can be hidden among the papillae. One supplied comparison graphic incorrectly labels Hopkins’ rose as an aeolid; this is noted rather than endorsed. ../../shared/media/asset-2a1a981e1a8e0bc5--IMG_3467.jpeg Dorid versus aeolid nudibranch anatomy — Kitty Turner. ../../shared/media/asset-cd38f502a51bf6bd--IMG_3468.jpeg Dorid versus aeolid comparison; source incorrectly identifies Hopkins’ rose as an aeolid. ../../shared/media/asset-2716d888f851c96f--IMG_3469.jpeg Branchial plumes (anal gills) and flat foot — Robin Agarwal. ../../shared/media/asset-3fd33c52e769a694--IMG_3470.jpeg Rhinophores among the papillae — Jerry Kirkhart. ../../shared/media/asset-7ddf650d12a6e651--IMG_3471.jpeg Full-body Hopkins’ rose, showing rhinophores and gills among pale papillae — iNaturalist. Hopkins’ rose nudibranch ../hopkins-rose-nudibranch/index.html Ceratodoris rosacea Pink dorid nudibranch whose northward appearances can indicate warmer ocean conditions; see the illustrated life cycle, anatomy, and color discussions in this Field Note. Length: approximately 1 inch (2–3 cm). Diet: red bryozoans, including Integripelta bilabiata. Predator: California aglaja (Navanax inermis). Habitat: rocky intertidal; source lists depths of 0–20 ft. Range: northern Baja California to central California, with warm-period sightings as far north as southern Oregon. Lifespan: source estimates 1–1.5 years; conservation status: Not Evaluated. Dorid gill plumes are hidden among papillae; rhinophores detect chemical cues. Prey-derived pigments contribute to its pink color.
