sections.title: May 28, 2026 (Bay Watch May 21–27) — Northern Elephant Seals • Deep-Sea Sleep • Conservation Comeback
sections.text: 2026-05-28-elephant-seals May 28, 2026 (Bay Watch May 21–27) Northern Elephant Seals • Deep-Sea Sleep • Conservation Comeback Northern elephant seal biology, breeding, migration and deep-sea sleep. Eleven original illustrated graphics, including conservation history. Bay Watch: May 21–27, 2026 — 32 sightings groups. Northern elephant seal — size and identification Northern elephant seals (Mirounga angustirostris) are the largest seals in the Northern Hemisphere. Southern elephant seals are larger; walruses rank third among pinnipeds. Males may reach about 13 ft and 4,400 lb; females about 10 ft and 1,300 lb. ../../shared/media/asset-bc4d2d7822e21690--size_compare.jpg Three largest pinnipeds — Peppermint Narwhal Creative. ../../shared/media/asset-43951da610ad3fd3--size_sketch.jpg Male, female and pup size comparison. Migration, feeding and diving Northern elephant seals range across the North Pacific from Alaska to Mexico. Adult males and females use different feeding areas; seals spend most of the year at sea and return to shore to breed and molt. Typical dives reach 1,000–2,000 ft, and a recorded dive reached 5,692 ft. They eat fish, squid and other deep-sea prey; white sharks and orcas are predators. ../../shared/media/asset-1a0051b4ea4be7ea--migration_map.jpg Male and female migration ranges. Breeding calendar, harems and pups Large males compete for access to females in breeding colonies. A female typically gives birth to one pup, nurses for roughly four weeks on fat-rich milk, and then weans it. Pups can grow from roughly 60–80 lb at birth to 250–350 lb at weaning. Some pups acquire additional milk and become unusually large 'super-weaners'; their later outcomes vary. ../../shared/media/asset-c6185696aabf48e5--calendar.jpg Annual breeding, molting and haul-out calendar. ../../shared/media/asset-125a4bbb92b0953b--rookery_scene.jpg Elephant seal harem and social structure. Foraging, body fat and buoyancy The source contrasts the diet of yearlings with adult feeding patterns. Elephant seals build fat reserves during long foraging trips; changes in body condition can change buoyancy and drifting behavior. The study graphic compares leaner and fatter seals; the graphic should not be interpreted as proving a single cause of survival or mortality. ../../shared/media/asset-9fa770d5f87c286a--diet_diagram.jpg Diet of a yearling northern elephant seal. ../../shared/media/asset-3895d93118cf6834--buoyancy_chart.jpg Body condition, buoyancy and drift-diving behavior. Deep-sea sleep and oxygen management Northern elephant seals can take brief sleep episodes during deep dives, sometimes around 15 minutes, and may total under two hours of sleep per day at sea, compared with much longer periods on land. Their oxygen stores and diving physiology support prolonged submergence. Unlike dolphins, true seals show bilateral rather than unihemispheric sleep. ../../shared/media/asset-dded438de5077361--sleep_diagram.jpg Comparison of marine mammal and human sleep patterns. Conservation: near-extinction and recovery Hunting for blubber drove northern elephant seals close to extinction in the nineteenth century; a remnant population survived around Guadalupe Island. Legal protections and reduced hunting allowed a major recovery. The source cites NOAA’s 2024 U.S. stock assessment at more than 200,000 seals; the older infographic shows a smaller historical estimate and should not be treated as the latest population count. ../../shared/media/asset-d8d7415dc63ff8f8--cons_basics.jpg Conservation history: historical hunting and decline — Peppermint Narwhal Creative. ../../shared/media/asset-a632a1f72984e42f--cons_comeback.jpg Conservation recovery timeline — Peppermint Narwhal Creative. ../../shared/media/asset-e13b365854bf974b--cons_success.jpg Recovery and continuing threats — Peppermint Narwhal Creative. Conservation: ongoing vigilance Despite their IUCN Least Concern classification, low genetic diversity from the historic bottleneck, entanglement, vessel strikes, interactions with people, disease risks and changing breeding-site conditions warrant continued monitoring. Disease scenarios, including avian influenza, are risks rather than evidence of a current outbreak in this population. Visitor guidance and wildlife rescue Northern Elephant Seal Mirounga angustirostris Largest true seal in the Northern Hemisphere; long-distance migrant, deep diver and a major conservation recovery story. ../../apps/northern-elephant-seal-pwa-v1.2-final-hub%20(2)/index.html Adult males may reach about 13 ft and 4,400 lb; females about 10 ft and 1,300 lb. Dives often reach 1,000–2,000 ft; a recorded maximum is 5,692 ft. The population recovered dramatically after nineteenth-century hunting. Conservation status: Least Concern; continued monitoring is important. Marine Mammal Cart — hard station The Marine Mammal Cart is launching as a hard station because of sensitive technology and props. Hard stations take priority over soft stations. Guides moving from one hard station to another should be relieved first. Consult or photograph the master schedule or ask other guides if unsure. Sunflower stars had been behind the scenes for well over a year. Exhibit staff consulted Sunflower Star Laboratory colleagues about tank conditions, biology and accurate bronze models. The email reports the exhibit is already installed; additional staff interpretation was anticipated. Activity on Monterey Bay Scattered humpback whales over the canyon, a few blue whales, black-footed albatross sightings, active dolphins and several passing orca pods were reported. Egg yolk jellies were especially abundant and appeared to be eaten by ocean sunfish (molas). Other jellyfish were also reported. Deceased humpback at Hopkins — observation, not diagnosis Whale-watching boats first spotted a dead humpback on Saturday. It later floated past Pacific Grove and drifted into Hopkins harbor seal beach cove, where it became trapped against rocks. The whale was belly-up and noticeably more swollen on a later sighting. The observer described a juvenile nearing maturity and a seemingly mostly white submerged tail, but no official identity or cause of death was available. Small round wounds were visible, with their origin uncertain. No obvious gear or residual entanglement injuries were visible, and the whale did not initially look underweight; these observations do not exclude any cause. Access for investigation was difficult. Harbor seals and potential predators Harbor seals appeared to leave their usual cove after the carcass arrived. A few young seals investigated and departed. The observer noted that the carcass could draw scavenging sharks, including large white sharks; nearby beach closures were described as precautionary. A salmon shark seen off Marina Beach may have been coincidental. The email judged orca scavenging less likely given visual access and cetaceans' lack of conventional smell; this was an interpretation, not a confirmed prediction. Whale-fall ecology and carcass management Decomposition gases can swell whale carcasses, but dramatic explosions are not typical or inevitable. Towing a carcass from this rocky, restricted cove could be hazardous, especially in forecast high winds. A decomposing whale can transfer nutrients and energy to beach, reef, seafloor or deep-sea ecosystems; this can temporarily change local ecological dynamics. Threats to humpback whales Entanglement and vessel strikes were identified as major threats, alongside predation, climate-driven food-web changes, ocean warming and acidification, and exposure to persistent contaminants such as PFAS. The email cites an international claim that a 10% ship-speed reduction was associated with 50% fewer whale collisions and 40% less ship noise; this numerical claim is retained as source attribution, not independently verified. Visitor conversations and emotional boundaries Guides uncomfortable discussing the dead humpback may politely decline, redirect to another topic or refer guests to another willing guide. The author offered to help answer questions. The source emphasizes avoiding speculation and respecting individual comfort levels. Related guide mentioned How did the whale die? No official cause of death had been determined. The belly-up position obscured the back, so possible ship-strike injuries could not be assessed. Small round wounds had uncertain origins; no obvious fishing gear or entanglement scars were seen, and the whale did not initially appear underweight. sections.text: 2026-06-18-24 June 18–24, 2026 Whale parasites, vessel strikes & returning humpbacks Blue and fin whales departed quickly as familiar humpbacks returned Preliminary necropsy findings from an Alaska fin whale vessel strike and regional conservation concerns Parasites Highlight: cookiecutter sharks, whalesuckers, whale barnacles and whale lice Eight supplied illustrated images, including two 'Where are the boops?' challenges Whale activity and familiar humpbacks Blue and fin whales were plentiful Monday but had largely departed by Tuesday, when only sparse humpbacks, a few dolphin pods and one lone male orca were found. Humpbacks later returned, including Snowy Owl, Aurora, Ratchet and Fingers. Alaska fin whale vessel strike and conservation The source reports preliminary necropsy findings that the pregnant fin whale was healthy, had a good blubber layer and died from blunt trauma associated with a vessel strike. It describes fin whales as 20% of known whales involved in vessel strikes; discusses regional vessel-speed and distance protections, Monterey cruise-ship restrictions, planned crab-trap restrictions in CDFW zones 4 and 5, and renewed Icelandic fin whaling. These are historical statements from the email, not independently verified current policies. Cookiecutter shark bites — Isistius brasiliensis Smalltooth cookiecutter sharks leave round bite wounds and scars on whales, sea lions, dolphins, other sharks, rays and fish. The source connects summertime marks on blue and fin whales with offshore feeding and nighttime vertical migration. ../../shared/media/asset-edd9d5ec2d0bbd07--IMG_3392.jpeg Fin whale displaying scars and skin damage from remoras and cookiecutter shark bites. Whalesuckers — Remora australis Whalesuckers attach with a modified dorsal-fin adhesive disk. The source describes their relationship with whales as often mutualistic or relatively harmless, although prolonged attachment can cause skin damage. Examples include blue whales, Risso’s dolphins and long-beaked common dolphins. ../../shared/media/asset-c9581b267211cbcb--IMG_3393.jpeg Blue whale with a single black whalesucker on the dorsal fin; below, a blue whale with many whalesuckers just below the dorsal fin. ../../shared/media/asset-54b172586520e9bd--IMG_3394.jpeg Risso’s dolphin with a faint whalesucker scar; below, a long-beaked common dolphin with a whalesucker scar. Whale barnacles and rabbit-ear gooseneck barnacles The source contrasts Coronula reginae, found on multiple baleen whale species, with Coronula diadema, most associated with humpbacks, and Cryptolepas rhachianecti on gray whales. Rabbit-ear barnacles (Conchoderma auritum) can grow on whale barnacles. Breaching may dislodge attached barnacles. ../../shared/media/asset-8940026ea5ec69fa--IMG_3395.jpeg Breaching humpback calf coated in whale barnacles and gooseneck barnacles. ../../shared/media/asset-eae8123213eff35a--IMG_3396.jpeg Healthy Coronula diadema barnacles growing along a humpback whale’s chin. ../../shared/media/asset-f78cedfed1d74f6b--IMG_3397.jpeg Gray whale with Cryptolepas rhachianecti barnacles; lower annotated image circles barnacle clusters. Whale lice — Cyamus boopis: two photo challenges Whale lice are crustaceans rather than insects. The source describes them grazing on algae and dead skin, remaining on whale hosts throughout their life cycles and transferring when whales come close. Challenge 1 and challenge 2 each preserve the original unmarked view followed by the marked answer in the same supplied image. ../../shared/media/asset-80f9762446c0fc02--IMG_3398.jpeg Whale lice challenge 1: Where are the boops? The source notes that coastal whales often have more external associates than offshore whales. sections.title: July 9–15, 2026 — Dolphin feeding frenzy, baby birds & Pseudo-nitzschia
sections.text: 2026-07-09-15 July 9–15, 2026 Dolphin feeding frenzy, baby birds & Pseudo-nitzschia Hundreds to more than a thousand common dolphins were gathering in Monterey Bay, with smaller pods sometimes passing the aquarium Baby western gulls and nesting Brandt’s and pelagic cormorants were visible around the aquarium Species Highlight: Pseudo-nitzschia, domoic acid and harmful algal blooms Wildlife-rescue warning signs and important local contact numbers were highlighted Dolphins and seabirds feeding together Large groups of several hundred to more than a thousand dolphins were being found most mornings. The groups often broke into smaller pods during the day, and some passed the aquarium. On Tuesday afternoon, more than a hundred dolphins were observed herding fish to the surface while pelicans plunge-dived and gulls grabbed fish near the surface. When conditions are good, guides can encourage visitors to look outside for visible activity. Babies around the aquarium Many young birds were visible around the aquarium, including western gull chicks at different stages of development. In addition to pelagic cormorants nesting beneath the aquarium, a Brandt’s cormorant was nesting there. Brandt’s can be distinguished by a thicker bill, yellow chin and a blue throat patch; pelagic cormorants have a more slender bill, red facial skin around the eye and chin, and can show stronger metallic green, blue and purple tones in good light. ../../shared/media/asset-1154cf3cd4637129--IMG_3355.jpeg Brandt’s cormorant nesting at the aquarium; the female’s blue throat patch is faintly visible. ../../shared/media/asset-732320e8868e04e9--IMG_3356.jpeg Western gull chick. Pseudo-nitzschia and harmful algal blooms Pseudo-nitzschia is a genus of marine diatoms. P. australis and P. multiseries are among the species capable of producing domoic acid and causing harmful algal blooms along the California coast. The presence of Pseudo-nitzschia alone does not mean conditions are dangerous; risk depends on abundance, species, toxin production and environmental conditions. Nutrient-rich upwelling can contribute to blooms, and domoic acid can move through the food web as plankton are eaten by fish, shellfish and other animals. ../../shared/media/asset-312b492bbd93cf7f--IMG_3357.jpeg Typical reproductive phases of Pseudo-nitzschia, including asexual and sexual reproduction. ../../shared/media/asset-ada016e625c82729--IMG_3358.jpeg Timeline and West Coast distribution associated with the persistent 2015 Pseudo-nitzschia harmful algal bloom and fisheries closures. Domoic acid through the food web Domoic acid can bioaccumulate in prey and expose seabirds and marine mammals that consume contaminated fish, squid or crustaceans. Neurological signs can include disorientation, abnormal behavior, seizures and, in severe cases, death. Domoic acid is heat-stable, so cooking does not reliably destroy it. In people, the recognized syndrome is amnesic shellfish poisoning (ASP), not paralytic shellfish poisoning. ../../shared/media/asset-ba81c2492733aa1b--IMG_3359.jpeg How domoic acid affects glutamate receptors and can produce neurological symptoms. ../../shared/media/asset-11daee627f87910c--IMG_3360.jpeg Harmful algal blooms and the food web: Pseudo-nitzschia can pass domoic acid through prey to wildlife and people. California sea lions and fetal exposure Research on California sea lions has raised concern about prenatal exposure as well as direct dietary exposure. Domoic acid can reach developing fetuses, and developmental exposure has been associated with neurological effects that may persist later in life. This makes recurring harmful algal blooms important not only for acute strandings but also for longer-term population health. ../../shared/media/asset-9d32c2f766326d0e--IMG_3361.jpeg Overlap between adult female California sea lion range, breeding areas and the general extent of Pseudo-nitzschia blooms. ../../shared/media/asset-bc73e2ecfad3750f--IMG_3362.jpeg Domoic acid exposure during pregnancy and possible long-term developmental effects in California sea lions. Wildlife warning signs Seabirds affected by illness or neurological toxins may appear confused, unusually passive or aggressive, show little fear of people, or wander into inappropriate places. Sea lions with suspected domoic-acid toxicosis may drool or foam, sway the head, have seizures, or hold the head abnormally upward or backward ('stargazing'). Keep people and dogs away from stranded marine mammals and never attempt to handle a sea lion. ../../shared/media/asset-a5b81ee6dc73e406--IMG_3363.jpeg Southern California public-alert poster illustrating neurological signs of domoic acid toxicosis. For Monterey Bay response, use the local contacts listed below. Pseudo-nitzschia ../pseudo-nitzschia/index.html Pseudo-nitzschia spp. A genus of needle-shaped marine diatoms that includes species capable of producing the neurotoxin domoic acid. Blooms can affect food webs, fisheries, seabirds, marine mammals and human seafood safety. 62 species were reported by the source update as recognized at the time, with 28 known to produce domoic acid P. australis is an important domoic-acid producer along the California coast These diatoms occur in marine and brackish waters and are especially relevant in nutrient-rich coastal waters Domoic acid can move through food webs and become concentrated in prey In humans, domoic-acid illness is called amnesic shellfish poisoning (ASP) Harmful algal blooms Domoic acid Upwelling and nutrients Food-web bioaccumulation Wildlife strandings Human seafood safety Sea-lion fetal exposure Is seeing Pseudo-nitzschia automatically dangerous? No. Pseudo-nitzschia can be present at low concentrations without causing a harmful event. Concern rises when toxin-producing species bloom and domoic acid enters the food web. sections.text: 2026-07-30-08-05 July 30–Aug 5, 2026 Macroalgae safety, abalone aquaculture & a special Bay guest Macroalgae toxicity to people is exceptionally rare; environmental contamination is different from toxins naturally produced by algae Toxic species are more characteristically associated with microalgae or phytoplankton, with Pseudo-nitzschia given as an example An abalone-farm visit highlighted growing interpretation and outreach plus sea urchins harvested from barrens as sustainable seafood Bay Watch included a blue whale, huge flocks of sooty shearwaters, fork-tailed petrel, purple-striped jellies and twin-sailed salps Can macroalgae be toxic? Macroalgae versus toxic microalgae In general, microalgae or phytoplankton are the group that includes toxic species, and only a small fraction of known species produce toxic substances. Pseudo-nitzschia was given as an example. Macroalgae are generally harmless to people except under specific circumstances. In the context of questions about edible seaweeds and kelps, the source says they are technically safe to eat, although they are not necessarily all tasty. Abalone farm visit and sustainable seafood Can seaweeds and kelps be toxic to people? The source says it is exceptionally rare for macroalgae to be toxic to people. They can absorb heavy metals or become coated in environmental toxins, but those contaminants are not toxins the macroalgae naturally produce. macroalgae seaweed kelp toxicity Are all seaweeds and kelps edible? In the context of this Field Note, the source says they are technically safe to eat, although they are not necessarily all tasty. sections.title: Aug 6–12, 2026 — Exhibit ledge ecology, rare seabirds & hydrophone mysteries
sections.text: 2026-08-06-12 Aug 6–12, 2026 Exhibit ledge ecology, rare seabirds & hydrophone mysteries Exhibit ledges highlighted as overlooked microhabitats rich in volunteer organisms from Monterey Bay Hydrophone recordings included orcas and gunshot-like sounds that could possibly be a North Pacific right whale Blue whales continued to appear as humpback peak season approached Rare and unusual birds included Buller’s and Manx shearwaters plus an unidentified masked-or-Nazca booby Car Week access reminder Volunteer Enrichment reported that the circle in front of the volunteer lounge would be barricaded through Aug. 16 to control traffic during Car Week. Volunteers whose drop-off or pick-up is affected were asked to plan accordingly. Hydrophone: orcas and possible right-whale sounds The hydrophone captured orcas on Tuesday night, described humorously as sounding like melancholy chicken crows. Gunshot-like sounds were also heard that could possibly have been a North Pacific right whale. The update did not confirm the identification. It noted that blue whales had been appearing and suggested krill could be present, which is also a food source for right whales. Seas the Summer in Moss Landing Four weekends remained in the Seas the Summer program. The Western Flyer Foundation planned Saturday activities such as seaweed pressing or cyanotyping and Sunday tours of the Western Flyer. A pop-up market featured local artists, Sunflower Star Laboratory offered tours, and nature or education books were being collected for a community giveaway table. Approaching humpback peak season and unusual seabirds Late September to mid-October is usually peak humpback season, although timing varies with conditions and migration. The update also reported more southern-origin birds: an unidentified booby that could have been masked or Nazca, Buller’s shearwaters that breed in New Zealand and range around the Pacific after fledging, and a Manx shearwater—common in the Atlantic but rare in the Pacific—feeding among sooty and pink-footed shearwaters. Mollusk class resources Exhibit Ledge Ecology — an overlooked microhabitat Exhibit ledges can support their own microhabitats, with encrusting coralline algae, small red and brown kelps, bryozoans, miniature anemones, top snails, limpets, chitons, sea slugs and other organisms. Larger animals may also use the ledges. Many organisms likely enter through the seawater intake as eggs or larvae, making some appearances seasonal and fleeting while anemones, bivalves, tegulas and limpets can be reliable long-term residents. ../../shared/media/asset-7be108d4e4678453--IMG_2867.jpeg An opalescent nudibranch on the ledge inside of the main Monterey Bay Habitats exhibit, taken with my crappy Motorola ../../shared/media/asset-f63a876a5501a7df--IMG_2868.jpeg I’m sorry, you wanted to look at a sevengill shark? Best I can do is one slug foot. ../../shared/media/asset-2c5a4f34f857290c--IMG_2869.jpeg A nudibranch’s egg ribbon, likely from an opalescent nudibranch ../../shared/media/asset-9b844bb19245cc28--IMG_2870.jpeg A chiton possibly grazing on the ledge of the Kelp Forest exhibit ../../shared/media/asset-717aac5f1a01e9a4--IMG_2871.jpeg So sorry for this terrible picture but I swear there is a tiny skeleton shrimp party in the green algae ../../shared/media/asset-05332b7e8a82d46d--IMG_2873.jpeg A limpet gently grazes on encrusted algae growth Why organisms settle on exhibit ledges The update proposed two possibilities for strong settlement on ledges: settlement cues and food. Coralline algae can act as a settlement cue for some local echinoderm larvae, helping indicate shallow coastal habitat. Ledges also provide food for grazers, omnivores and scavengers, while carnivores can find prey such as hydroids and small anemones. Skeleton shrimp can reproduce on exhibit because their larval stages remain in the mother’s brood pouch and emerge as miniature adults rather than requiring a pelagic stage. ../../shared/media/asset-4d7635af67d3f236--IMG_2874.jpeg An opalescent nudibranch cruising among small white anemones ../../shared/media/asset-b741e9d8704a02e7--IMG_2876.jpeg A small spotted triopha nudibranch crawling up the Monterey Bay Habitats exhibit window Ledges as accessible observation stations Not every animal on a ledge is a volunteer organism. Monitoring ledges can reveal cryptic or temporary exhibit animals in places where guests can see them more easily. The update emphasized ledges as accessible observation sites for children and guests who may have difficulty standing or searching deeper into an exhibit. ../../shared/media/asset-80b0c96b94623a37--IMG_2877.jpeg A California sea hare on the edge of the ledge ../../shared/media/asset-b1db1b549a2c88c2--IMG_2878.jpeg A painted greenling hiding behind kelp fronds on the second story window ledge of the Kelp Forest exhibit ../../shared/media/asset-e9e0af345fc4b30e--IMG_2882.jpeg A California moray eel resting on the ledge with a rockfish pillow ../../shared/media/asset-0ddc6e6b4b55ea55--IMG_2883.jpeg An older California sheephead female in the process of changing into a male Camouflage, feeding and interpretation on the ledge The ledges offer opportunities to interpret adaptations. Limpets graze algae; falsejingles, chitons and some snails can become algae-encrusted and better camouflaged; aeolid nudibranchs such as opalescent nudibranchs resemble parts of their prey and can retain consumed stinging cells for defense. Fish using swim bladders must actively move down the water column to rest near a ledge. Close animals can also become live models for discussing fish morphology and habitat adaptations. ../../shared/media/asset-bbd4d6a226d73e44--IMG_2884.jpeg A false jingle with an algae encrusted hat ../../shared/media/asset-5afe045acf5fb1f9--IMG_2885.jpeg A small flatfish on the ledge of the Kelp Forest exhibit ../../shared/media/asset-dfd821c14f7227eb--IMG_2886.jpeg A bat star on the ledge of the Kelp Forest exhibit Why the open-sea system matters The update closed by emphasizing that these small ledge ecosystems are made possible by the aquarium’s open-sea system. Organisms arriving from Monterey Bay can create rich, changing communities that reflect the bay’s diversity and seasonal changes, rewarding careful observation by guides and guests. sections.text: 2026-08-20-26 Aug 20–26, 2026 Timber Fire, marine impacts & scarred short-beaked common dolphins Short-beaked common dolphins increasingly seen around Monterey Bay Tooth-rake, remora and probable Pacific lamprey scarring observed Topic Highlight: how wildfire smoke, ash, runoff and fire suppressants can affect the ocean Bay Watch included humpback and blue whales plus both common-dolphin species Rotation and hard-station reminder The update reminded volunteers to keep all hard stations staffed through every block, alternate hard and soft assignments when possible, arrive 3–5 minutes early when moving from a soft station to a hard station, and call Center for an IP specialist if relief is five minutes late or more. Short-beaked common dolphin scarring More short-beaked common dolphins were reported around the bay. They showed extensive tooth-rake marks as well as remora scarring and small circular scars interpreted in the source update as most likely from Pacific lamprey; the scars were considered too small for cookiecutter shark bites. Topic Highlight — Wildfires and ocean health Prompted by the visible Timber Fire in Big Sur, the update explored how wildfire smoke, ash, post-fire runoff and fire-suppression chemicals can affect coastal ecosystems. It discussed particulate matter, reduced sunlight, pH changes, nutrients, heavy metals, PFAS, dissolved organic matter, plankton responses, harmful algal blooms, food-web effects and potential impacts on marine mammals. The update also described KelpFire, a research effort studying wildfire effects on California kelp ecosystems. Fire suppressants and runoff The update described common fire-retardant ingredients and concerns about concentrated nutrients, ammonia, heavy metals and runoff. It emphasized a second pulse of material after winter rains wash ash-enriched soil into streams and the ocean, potentially encouraging plankton blooms or harmful algal blooms. Marine mammals and cascading effects The source connected wildfire-driven changes with possible bioaccumulation, reduced immune response, habitat degradation, altered prey, stress and reproductive effects. It cited observations and research involving sea otters, sea lions, dolphins and whales while noting that ocean effects can be difficult to attribute to a single cause. Why can’t whales molt well in cold water? In cold water, whales can reduce blood flow near the skin to conserve heat. Reduced skin perfusion and turnover can slow epidermal shedding. Human water-induced wrinkling is an active autonomic vasoconstriction response, especially in the thick skin of fingers and toes. Cetaceans do not use that same specialized response, and their skin is adapted for continuous aquatic life. whales skin physiology Did baleen whales lose echolocation? Current evidence supports sophisticated biosonar evolving in the toothed-whale lineage after toothed and baleen whales diverged. Offshore forms can show spinal patterns associated with high-speed swimming, while riverine/coastal forms can emphasize maneuverability. ../../shared/media/asset-57ba856b9eed6807--IMG_2360.jpeg Cetacean vertebral regionalization from shallow-water to open-ocean forms. Northern Elephant Seal Mirounga angustirostris Animals ANIMAL VOLUNTEER_GUIDE_REFERENCE 1.2 2026-06-28 Guide-friendly animal page for northern elephant seal size, migration, breeding, deep diving, underwater sleep, conservation comeback, and beach-safe visitor messaging. size_compare Graphic comparing the southern elephant seal, northern elephant seal, and walrus by size. Pinniped size comparison: northern elephant seals are among the largest pinnipeds. size_sketch Watercolor sketch of a male northern elephant seal, female, and pup with notes on size, diving, and nursing. Male, female, and pup comparison with field-guide style notes. migration_map Hand-drawn map showing northern elephant seal migration range in the eastern North Pacific. Migration range map showing male and female foraging areas and breeding sites. cons_basics Conservation comeback graphic showing northern elephant seal range, migration routes, and historical hunting threat. Conservation basics: long migration, former hunting pressure, and range. rookery_scene Illustrated northern elephant seal rookery with alpha male, females, pups, super weaners, and peripheral males. Rookery social structure: alpha male, females, pups, super weaners, and peripheral males. calendar Circular annual calendar showing adult male breeding, adult female breeding, pups, molting, and juvenile haul-out periods. Annual cycle: breeding, pups, molting, and juvenile haul-out. diet_diagram Diet diagram showing lanternfish, hake, ratfish, and squid around a young elephant seal. Diet diagram: fish dominate the diet in this example, with squid also represented. sleep_diagram Diagram comparing unihemispheric sleep in cetaceans and some otariids with bilateral sleep in phocid seals and humans. Sleep comparison: true seals can use bilateral sleep, unlike dolphins that often sleep one hemisphere at a time. buoyancy_chart Scientific chart showing elephant seal drift dive timing, body fat percentage, negative buoyancy, and positive buoyancy. Buoyancy and drift-diving pattern as body condition changes during foraging. cons_comeback Conservation comeback timeline for northern elephant seals showing protection, recovery, and Marine Mammal Protection Act context. Comeback timeline: protection and population recovery after heavy hunting pressure. cons_success Conservation success graphic showing northern elephant seal population growth, Least Concern status, and modern threats. Recovery success, current Least Concern status, and ongoing threats. Adult females commonly reach about 10 feet; adult males commonly reach about 13 feet. Adult females commonly weigh around 1,300 pounds; adult males commonly weigh around 4,000–4,400 pounds, with some larger individuals reported. Fish, squid, and deep-sea prey; adults may also eat small sharks, rays, and chimaeras. Great white sharks and orcas are important natural predators. Eastern North Pacific; mostly open ocean, with breeding, pupping, molting, and resting on beaches and islands. Often deep-diving; many dives reach hundreds to thousands of feet, and some exceed 5,000 feet. Eastern North Pacific, broadly from Alaska to Mexico, with major breeding colonies in California and Baja California. Can live up to about 19 years; lifespan varies by sex and survival pressure. IUCN: Least Concern. Protected in the U.S. under the Marine Mammal Protection Act. A northern elephant seal can take underwater naps while sinking slowly through the deep ocean. That is a very big animal taking a very quiet power nap! Picture a California beach in winter: giant males rumble, females call to their pups, and young seals wiggle through the sand. Northern elephant seals may look sleepy on shore, but they are ocean athletes built for long migrations and deep dives.

Most of the year they are far offshore, hunting in dark water where lanternfish, squid, and other deep-sea animals live. Then they return to land for the big energy events: breeding, nursing pups, molting, and resting.

Their comeback is one of the great marine mammal recovery stories. After being hunted nearly to extinction for oil, northern elephant seals rebounded under protection. But their recovery came from a very small remnant population, so genetic diversity remains a long-term concern. Northern elephant seals are not usually an exhibit animal at Monterey Bay Aquarium. Visitors may see them seasonally at protected coastal haul-outs and rookeries in California, including sites such as Año Nuevo and Piedras Blancas.

At MBA, this app is best used as a marine mammal cart, coastal wildlife, conservation, or beach-safety conversation companion. Mostly open ocean in the eastern North Pacific. On land, they use beaches, islands, and rookeries for pupping, breeding, molting, and resting. Broadly Alaska to Mexico. Many major breeding sites are in California and Baja California. Often deep-diving; many foraging dives are in the mesopelagic, or twilight zone. Some dives exceed 5,000 feet. Fish, squid, and deep-sea prey. Commonly reported prey include lanternfish, hake, squid, small sharks, rays, and chimaeras. Great white sharks and orcas. They spend much of the year at sea and return to land for breeding, pupping, molting, and resting. Males compete for breeding access to females. Females nurse pups for a short, intense period before returning to sea. Huge oxygen stores in blood and muscle help support long dives. Thick blubber stores energy and helps with insulation and buoyancy. Large eyes and sensitive whiskers help them hunt in dim deep water. Males have an inflatable nose, or proboscis, used to make loud breeding-season calls. True seals can enter bilateral sleep during deep drift dives, meaning both brain hemispheres sleep at once. Can live up to about 19 years, though many young animals do not survive their first years. IUCN: Least Concern. U.S. protection: Marine Mammal Protection Act. Northern elephant seals can sleep during deep drift dives at sea. Their sleep is different from dolphins and many whales. Dolphins often use unihemispheric sleep, where one side of the brain sleeps while the other remains more alert. True seals, including elephant seals, can use bilateral sleep, where both brain hemispheres sleep at once.

This matters because elephant seals spend months at sea. They cannot simply climb onto land every night. Instead, they combine diving, drifting, resting, and foraging in a way that lets them survive in the open ocean. As elephant seals forage, their body condition changes. A leaner seal may be negatively buoyant and sink more easily. A fatter seal with more stored energy may become more positively buoyant. Scientists can use drift dives and body angle to understand whether a seal is gaining condition during a foraging trip.

This is a useful guide story because it connects deep diving, blubber, energy storage, migration, and survival. Northern elephant seals follow a strong annual rhythm. Adults return to land for breeding and pupping, then go back to sea to feed. They later return for molting, when old skin and hair are shed. Juveniles also haul out seasonally.

On the rookery, dominant males may control access to groups of females. Peripheral males remain near the edge and may try to breed when opportunities occur. Pups nurse for only a few weeks, gaining fat quickly before their mothers return to sea. Northern elephant seals were heavily hunted in the 1800s for oil. By the late 1800s, the species was reduced to a very small remnant population and was thought by many to be extinct. Protection in Mexico and the United States allowed the population to recover.

Today, the species is listed as Least Concern, but that does not mean humans can ignore them. Modern concerns include fishing gear entanglement, boat strikes, disturbance at haul-outs, limited genetic diversity from the historical bottleneck, and the effects of severe weather and climate change on breeding sites. Resting seals on beaches need space. A seal that lifts its head, looks toward people, vocalizes, or moves away may already be disturbed. Disturbance costs energy that seals need for molting, nursing, migration, and survival.

Best visitor message: stay back, obey signs and barriers, keep dogs away, never touch or feed a marine mammal, and contact trained responders if an animal appears injured or in distress. Northern elephant seals connect visitors to deep-sea food webs, migration, climate, sleep science, predator-prey relationships, and conservation recovery. They are also a memorable way to teach respectful wildlife viewing: resting is survival behavior. Where can I see northern elephant seals? They are usually seen at coastal haul-outs and rookeries, not inside the Aquarium. In California, well-known viewing areas include Año Nuevo and Piedras Blancas. Always stay behind signs and barriers. Why are the males so much bigger than the females? Breeding is competitive. Large males fight and display for access to breeding areas, so size can help a male win space on the beach. Females are much smaller but invest huge energy into nursing pups. What do they eat? They eat fish, squid, and other deep-sea animals. Adults may also eat small sharks, rays, and chimaeras. Much of their hunting happens far offshore and deep below the surface. How deep can they dive? Many dives are hundreds to thousands of feet deep, and some have been recorded deeper than 5,000 feet. Do they really sleep underwater? Yes. Research shows elephant seals can take short sleep dives at sea. True seals can sleep with both brain hemispheres at once, unlike dolphins, which often sleep one side of the brain at a time. Are they dangerous? They are wild, very large animals and can move faster than people expect on sand. The safest and most respectful choice is to keep your distance, follow signs, and never approach or touch a seal. Are they endangered? The IUCN lists northern elephant seals as Least Concern, and their recovery from near-extinction is a conservation success story. They are still protected, and low genetic diversity, disturbance, entanglement, and changing ocean conditions remain concerns. What is a super weaner? A super weaner is a pup that gets extra milk, sometimes by nursing from more than one female. It can become extremely heavy, which sounds helpful, but too much buoyancy may make early diving harder. Why do they look so awkward on land? Northern elephant seals are true seals. Their rear flippers are built for swimming and do not rotate under the body for walking. They move on land by wriggling and pushing, but in water they are powerful and efficient. How can visitors help? Give resting seals plenty of space, obey beach signs, keep dogs away, reduce plastic and fishing-line waste, and call a trained rescue group if you see a marine mammal that appears injured or in distress. Great opening line: “They look like beach potatoes, but they are deep-ocean athletes.” Point out the contrast: awkward on land, graceful and efficient at sea. Use the annual cycle: breed, forage, molt, forage again. They are on a tight energy budget. Connect to the deep sea: lanternfish and squid are part of the twilight-zone food web. Use the sleep diagram to compare true seals, sea lions, dolphins, and humans. Use the buoyancy chart to explain how scientists can infer body condition from drift dives. Avoid saying only “rescued from extinction.” Better: “protected after being hunted to a tiny remnant population.” Beach-safety message: resting is survival behavior. A seal that lifts its head or moves away has already been disturbed. For Monterey County marine mammal distress reports, use the current local rescue hotline only after verifying it with MBA-approved volunteer materials.   surfaces. The open sea is different because it is primarily defined by

sections.title: Standard coloration and Brownell morph
sections.text: Standard coloration and Brownell morph The Brownell morph has a distinctive dark lateral patch framed by a contrasting light stripe. It is a recurring coloration pattern, not albinism. sections.title: Range, habitat, prey and diving
sections.text: Range, habitat, prey and diving Found across the North Pacific from Mexico to East Asia and north to Alaska and Russia, in nearshore and offshore waters. The source lists herring, sardines, anchovies, market squid, whiting, capelin, chub mackerel and other fishes and squid. Diving caution:  The author questions online claims of dives to 3,280 ft and suggests nighttime vertical prey migration as a possible explanation for deepwater prey. A proposed 600–1,000 ft dive range is speculation in the email, not a confirmed limit.

sections.title: Regional stock and returning pods
sections.text: Regional stock and returning pods The March 2026 author cites approximately 21,000–35,000 animals in the California–Oregon–Washington stock and describes it as stable. Photo-identification suggests pods revisit Monterey Bay, but finer-scale site fidelity needs more study.

sections.title: Reproduction and calf development
sections.text: Reproduction and calf development According to the shift update, mating activity is especially evident in late summer and fall; gestation lasts 9–12 months; newborn calves average 3 ft and 30 lb. Weaning generally occurs at 12 months but may extend to 18 months. Females may calve every 2–5 years. The author reports maturity at 8–10 years for females and 10–11 years for males.

sections.title: Mixed-species associations and superpods
sections.text: Mixed-species associations and superpods Pacific white-sided dolphins frequently mix with northern right whale dolphins and sometimes other marine mammals. Temporary superpods can exceed 1,000 individuals. Predator avoidance, shared feeding, mating and social benefits are hypotheses rather than settled explanations. Mixed-species association and vigilance illustration, marked @whalescientists.

sections.title: Visitor questions
sections.text: Visitor questions Why do some look different?  A recurring Brownell coloration morph differs from the usual pattern. Why are two dolphin species together?  Possible advantages include safety and feeding, but no single cause is confirmed. Do these dolphins migrate?  The source describes regional movements in response to food rather than long seasonal migrations.

sections.title: Identification
sections.text: Identification Stargazers are marine fishes whose eyes and upward-facing mouths sit on top of broad heads. The family Uranoscopidae includes species from shallow and deep seas worldwide. The source introduces an Astroscopus stargazer in the aquarium's tube-anemone tank.

sections.title: Sand-burial and breathing
sections.text: Sand-burial and breathing Stargazers use strong pectoral fins to bury themselves rapidly in sediment. Their upper-head breathing openings and fringes help exclude sand while they wait for prey.

sections.title: Ambush hunting
sections.text: Ambush hunting They lie hidden until a fish, small crustacean or other bottom-dwelling invertebrate comes close, then strike rapidly. Some stargazers use a worm-like oral lure.

sections.title: Venom and electricity
sections.text: Venom and electricity Venomous spines occur near the gill covers. Some Astroscopus stargazers also generate electric discharges using modified eye muscles. The source describes these as defensive or predatory adaptations.

sections.title: Development
sections.text: Development Eggs laid near the seabed rise into the water column. Planktonic larvae later settle as their bodies and upward-facing eyes develop. The source compares this developmental change with flatfish.

sections.title: Visitor interpretation
sections.text: Visitor interpretation Look for the animal's eyes protruding above the sand and discuss ambush camouflage. Avoid handling; the spines can cause injury. Source text contributed by Michael Gilmartin and shared by Sallie.

sections.title: CHAPTER 0 What Is Life? Definition and boundary
sections.text:
CHAPTER 0 What Is Life? Definition and boundary 
 
 Life is a self-maintaining system that uses energy, responds to its environment, reproduces, and has the capacity to evolve. 
 There is no universally accepted single definition. Scientists instead look for a combination of characteristics. 

 
 HORGASM: seven characteristics 
 
 H Homeostasis  regulates internal conditions. 
 O Organization  uses one or more cells. 
 R Reproduction  continues a living lineage. 
 G Growth  builds structure through controlled processes. 
 A Adaptation  occurs in populations over generations. 
 S Response to stimuli  detects and reacts to change. 
 M Metabolism  transforms energy and matter. 
 
 

 
 Are viruses alive? 
 Viruses carry genetic information and evolve, but they are not cells and cannot independently maintain homeostasis, metabolize, grow, or reproduce. They use the machinery of living host cells. Guide line:  “A virus brings instructions, but the living cell supplies the factory.”

sections.title: CHAPTER 1 The Earliest Earth 4.54–3.4 billion years ago
sections.text:
CHAPTER 1 The Earliest Earth 4.54–3.4 billion years ago 
 

 
 Formation of the Early Earth 
 
 
 Earth formed about 4.54 billion years ago. 
 The young Earth was extremely hot, with a largely molten surface. 
 As the planet cooled, crust and oceans formed. 
 The atmosphere was rich in carbon dioxide, nitrogen, water vapor, and other volcanic gases. 
 There was virtually no free atmospheric oxygen. 
 
 Guide discussion:  Without oxygen, early life used metabolisms very different from the oxygen-dependent metabolism familiar to us today. 
 
 

 
 The Earliest Evidence of Life 
 
 About 3.8–3.7 billion years ago Possible Greenland evidence Chemical and structural evidence has been interpreted as biological, but some claims remain debated. 
 About 3.5–3.4 billion years ago Stronger microbial evidence Ancient rocks from South Africa and Western Australia preserve evidence consistent with microbial communities, including stromatolite-like structures. 
 
 

 
 Stromatolites: visible evidence of a microbial world 
 Stromatolites are layered structures built as microbial communities trap sediment and precipitate minerals. Some ancient examples are among Earth’s oldest visible evidence of life. Living stromatolites still form in a few modern environments. 
 

 
 Life Was Microbial 
 
 For nearly two billion years, Earth was inhabited almost entirely by single-celled organisms—bacteria and archaea. 
 Not yet: plants animals fish trees dinosaurs 
 Complex visible life occupies only the most recent portion of Earth’s history. 
 
 

 
 Why Earth could support long-term evolution 
 Earth supplied persistent liquid water, carbon-rich chemistry, minerals, environmental gradients, and continuous energy sources. These conditions did not guarantee life, but they allowed complex chemistry and long-term evolution to continue.

sections.text:
CHAPTER 2 From Chemistry Toward Life Hypotheses and evidence 
 

 
 Prebiotic Chemistry 
 
 Before biology, Earth contained chemical ingredients capable of forming more complex organic molecules. 
 Liquid water and early oceans Carbon-, nitrogen-, sulfur-, and phosphorus-containing compounds Mineral surfaces that could concentrate or organize reactions Energy from ultraviolet light, lightning, volcanism, and hydrothermal systems 
 
 

 
 Hydrothermal Vent Hypothesis 
 One leading family of hypotheses places early chemical evolution near seafloor hydrothermal systems. Mineral pores could have provided compartments, catalytic surfaces, chemical gradients, hydrogen, and carbon dioxide. This remains a hypothesis rather than a confirmed birthplace of life. 
 

 
 RNA World? — Hypothesis 
 RNA can both store information and catalyze certain chemical reactions. The RNA World hypothesis proposes that RNA-like systems played a major role before the modern DNA–RNA–protein system evolved. Not established:  Scientists have not reconstructed a complete self-sustaining RNA-based organism from early-Earth conditions. 
 

 
 Protocells 
 Fatty molecules can spontaneously form membrane-like compartments. Protocells are proposed chemical systems in which a boundary, heredity, and metabolism began operating together. They were not necessarily true modern cells. 
 

 
 FUCA? — First Universal Common Ancestor 
 
 FUCA is a hypothetical concept for a very early ancestor—or population of primitive systems—near the transition from chemistry to biology. 
 It may not have been a single organism. Its biology is unknown. It may predate the fully developed genetic and cellular machinery inferred for LUCA. It remains an active and highly theoretical area of research. 
 
 

 
 Many Early Lineages 
 The earliest living world probably contained many experimental lineages. Most became extinct and left no living descendants. LUCA was therefore not necessarily the only organism alive; it is the ancestral population through which all surviving cellular life is connected.

 FUCA is a hypothetical concept for a very early ancestor—or population of primitive systems—near the transition from chemistry to biology. 
 It may not have been a single organism. Its biology is unknown. It may predate the fully developed genetic and cellular machinery inferred for LUCA. It remains an active and highly theoretical area of research.

sections.title: Many Early Lineages
sections.text:
Many Early Lineages 
 The earliest living world probably contained many experimental lineages. Most became extinct and left no living descendants. LUCA was therefore not necessarily the only organism alive; it is the ancestral population through which all surviving cellular life is connected.

sections.title: CHAPTER 3 LUCA and the First Great Branches Universal inheritance
sections.text:
CHAPTER 3 LUCA and the First Great Branches Universal inheritance 
 

 
 LUCA — Last Universal Common Ancestor 
 
 LUCA was not necessarily the first life, one individual, or a modern-looking cell. It represents the last ancestral population shared by all cellular organisms alive today. 
 
 Likely present DNA and RNA Ribosomes and protein synthesis A genetic code Cell membranes ATP-based energy chemistry Core metabolic pathways 
 Not yet present as eukaryotic organelles Nucleus Mitochondria Chloroplasts 
 
 LUCA’s exact age, habitat, membrane structure, and metabolism remain debated. 
 
 

 
 Bacteria 
 Bacteria became one of the major cellular lineages. Their later diversity included cyanobacteria, which evolved oxygen-producing photosynthesis, and the alphaproteobacterial lineage related to the ancestor of mitochondria. 
 

 
 Archaea 
 
 Archaea form another major cellular lineage. Many were first recognized in extreme environments: 
 hot springs hydrothermal vents acidic waters hypersaline waters 
 Archaea also live throughout ordinary soils, oceans, sediments, and animal microbiomes. Many use chemical energy rather than sunlight. Modern evidence links an Asgard-archaea-related lineage closely to the host side of eukaryotic origins.

sections.title: CHAPTER 4 Oxygen: Earth’s First Great Pollution Planetary transformation
sections.text:
CHAPTER 4 Oxygen: Earth’s First Great Pollution Planetary transformation 
 

 
 Cyanobacteria Changed the Planet 
 Cyanobacteria evolved oxygen-producing photosynthesis. They used sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide to build sugars and released oxygen. Sunlight + CO₂ + H₂O → Sugars + O₂ 
 

 
 Why oxygen was initially a pollutant 
 Early organisms evolved in an oxygen-free world. Oxygen is highly reactive and could damage their molecules. For many anaerobic microbes, it was toxic. 
 

 
 Why oxygen did not accumulate immediately 
 Oxygen first reacted with dissolved iron, volcanic gases, rocks, and other reduced materials. These oxygen sinks absorbed it before sustained atmospheric accumulation became possible. 
 

 
 The Great Oxidation Event 
 Beginning around 2.4 billion years ago, oxygen accumulated persistently in the atmosphere. Many anaerobic lineages declined or became restricted to oxygen-free habitats, while other organisms evolved detoxification and oxygen-using metabolism. 
 

 
 Oxygen levels rose in stages 
 The Great Oxidation Event did not immediately create modern oxygen levels. Oxygen continued changing over immense spans of time, with later oceanic and atmospheric increases helping support larger, more active multicellular organisms. 
 

 
 Why oxygen became an opportunity 
 Aerobic respiration can release large amounts of usable energy from food. Organisms able to exploit oxygen gained access to a powerful energy source.

sections.title: CHAPTER 5 The Rise of Eukaryotes Ancient partnerships
sections.text:
CHAPTER 5 The Rise of Eukaryotes Ancient partnerships 
 

 
 Endosymbiosis I: the origin of mitochondria 
 
 An archaea-related host lineage formed a lasting partnership with an alphaproteobacterial cell. Instead of one partner destroying the other, the relationship became permanent. The bacterial partner evolved into the mitochondrion. 
 Archaea-related host ＋ alphaproteobacterial partner → mitochondria-bearing eukaryotic lineage 
 The exact sequence by which the nucleus, cytoskeleton, internal membranes, and mitochondrial partnership assembled remains an active area of research. 
 
 

 
 Why mitochondria matter 
 Mitochondria use oxygen-dependent chemistry to generate ATP, the immediately usable energy currency of cells. This energy system helped support larger genomes, active transport, movement, and cellular complexity. 
 

 
 All plants have mitochondria 
 Plant cells perform photosynthesis in chloroplasts and cellular respiration in mitochondria. Animals have mitochondria but no chloroplasts. Plants have both. 
 

 
 Endosymbiosis II: the origin of chloroplasts 
 
 A mitochondria-bearing eukaryote formed a second permanent partnership, this time with a cyanobacterium. That cyanobacterium evolved into the primary chloroplast. 
 eukaryotic host with mitochondria ＋ cyanobacterium → photosynthetic eukaryote with chloroplasts 
 This primary event gave rise to the plastid lineage inherited by red algae, green algae, and land plants.

sections.title: CHAPTER 6 Algae and the Green Lineage Not one single group
sections.text:
CHAPTER 6 Algae and the Green Lineage Not one single group 
 

 
 “Algae” are not one evolutionary branch 
 Algae are multiple photosynthetic eukaryotic lineages with different evolutionary histories. The word describes a lifestyle and appearance more than a single natural group. 
 

 
 Red algae 
 Red algae descend from the primary chloroplast-bearing lineage and form their own ancient branch of photosynthetic eukaryotes. 
 

 
 Green algae and land plants 
 Land plants evolved from within the green lineage. Green algae are therefore the closest algal relatives of land plants, although “green algae” themselves include several branches. 
 

 
 Brown algae and secondary endosymbiosis 
 Brown algae did not inherit chloroplasts directly from the original cyanobacterial partnership. Their ancestors engulfed a red-algal cell and retained its chloroplast—a later process called secondary endosymbiosis. This is one reason algae do not form a single branch. 
 

 
 From green algae to land plants 
 
 Moving onto land required a series of evolutionary innovations. They did not all appear at once or in one straight line. 
 
 green-algal ancestors → embryo protection → cuticle → stomata → vascular tissue → true roots, stems, and leaves → seeds → flowers

sections.title: CHAPTER 7 The Branching Tree of Life Common ancestry
sections.text:
CHAPTER 7 The Branching Tree of Life Common ancestry 
 

 
 Evolution is a tree, not a ladder 
 No living species is the goal or top of evolution. Every organism is a surviving twig on a branching tree. Humans, jellyfish, kelp, bacteria, and birds all have equally long evolutionary histories extending back to shared ancestors. 
 

 
 Animals 
 Animals form one branch of eukaryotes. Early animals evolved in the ocean before plants colonized land. Animals did not evolve from plants. 
 

 
 Fungi 
 Fungi form a separate eukaryotic branch and are more closely related to animals than to plants. 
 

 
 Plants and animals are separate branches 
 Plants and animals diverged from much older eukaryotic ancestors. Photosynthetic algae existed before animals, but land plants appeared after early animals were already present. 
 

 
 What the common ancestor tells us 
 When two organisms are compared, the key question is not which is “higher.” It is where their lineages last shared an ancestral population and what traits were already present at that point. 
 

 
 Taxonomic rank versus evolutionary divergence 
 Kingdom, phylum, class, and other ranks help organize organisms, but ranks are human categories. The branching point—the last common ancestor—is the scientific event the Tree of Life Explorer should emphasize. 
 

 Transition to organism comparison:  “Choose any two organisms. We will trace their branches backward until they meet, then identify what their common ancestor likely possessed.”

sections.title: GUIDE SUPPORT Suggested Talk Sequence 1–5 minutes
sections.text:
GUIDE SUPPORT Suggested Talk Sequence 1–5 minutes 
 
 
 Begin:  “What makes something alive?” 
 Test the boundary:  Use viruses as the discussion case. 
 Set the scene:  Young Earth had oceans but virtually no atmospheric oxygen. 
 Establish scale:  Life remained microbial for nearly two billion years. 
 Create the turning point:  Cyanobacteria released a toxic pollutant—oxygen. 
 Introduce partnership:  A bacterium became the mitochondrion inside an archaea-related host lineage. 
 Add photosynthesis:  A later cyanobacterium became the chloroplast. 
 Finish with branching:  Animals, fungi, plants, and algae occupy different branches. 
 Open the Explorer:  Compare two organisms and find where their histories meet.

sections.title: REFERENCE Scientific Cautions Guide level
sections.text:
REFERENCE Scientific Cautions Guide level 
 
 
 RNA World, protocells, hydrothermal origins, and FUCA are hypotheses or theoretical frameworks. 
 LUCA was likely a population and was not necessarily the first life. 
 The exact order of mitochondrial acquisition, nucleus formation, and internal membrane evolution remains debated. 
 Brown algae acquired their plastids through secondary endosymbiosis involving a red-algal ancestor. 
 Adaptation occurs across populations and generations; individuals do not evolve because they “need” to. 
 Taxonomic ranks do not always correspond neatly to equal evolutionary depths.

sections.text: cookiecutter Cookiecutter Shark Isistius brasiliensis #FFF0E8 Broad Host tag-broad broad A small deep-sea shark that bites circular plugs from much larger animals — its name describes exactly what the wound looks like. Not a true parasite in the classical sense, but functionally parasitic: it takes tissue and leaves a scar. Cookiecutters migrate to the surface at night during vertical migration alongside other deep-sea organisms. Whales feeding over deep water in summer are especially exposed. Bites leave large, round scars that persist for life. sections.title: Whalesucker
sections.text: remora Whalesucker Remora australis #E8F4F0 Mutualist tag-mutualist whale mutualist A remora species with a strong preference for whales as hosts. Not a true parasite — the relationship leans mutualistic. The whalesucker grazes dead skin and external parasites from its host whale, providing cleaning services in exchange for a free ride and predator refuge. They attach via a modified dorsal fin that acts as an adhesive disk. Long-term attachment can cause heavier skin damage at the contact site. Blue whales this week showed everything from a single sucker on the dorsal fin to dense clusters below it. sections.title: Humpback Barnacle
sections.text: coronula Humpback Barnacle Coronula diadema #EBF4F4 Host-Specific tag-specific specific mutualist Almost exclusively found on humpback whales — rarely documented on other species. Large accumulations develop over time, particularly around the chin, flippers, and flukes. Humpbacks can shed clusters through behaviors like breaching. Despite the parasite label, harm is generally limited to added drag and weight. The barnacles themselves can be parasitized by gooseneck barnacles, creating a stacked parasite-on-parasite arrangement. Like all whale barnacles, they filter-feed while getting transport to productive feeding grounds. The relationship is commensal at worst and may offer mild host benefit through the secondary organisms they support. Its two fleshy lobes at the top of the stalk resemble rabbit ears. This creates a true layered parasitic system: the whale hosts Coronula barnacles, which in turn host Conchoderma. The gooseneck draws nutrients from the whale barnacle rather than directly from the whale. sections.text: whalelice Whale Lice Cyamus boopis #E8EFF8 Host-Specific tag-specific specific Not insects — whale lice are crustaceans. Despite the name, they are weakly parasitic at best, grazing on algae growth and dead skin from whale surfaces. Their entire lifecycle plays out on a single whale host. Transfer between whales occurs only during close contact. Because opportunities to switch hosts are rare, whale lice populations are highly host-specific. On humpbacks, look for them tucked into skin folds, barnacle margins, and around the rostrum. sections.title: Quick Guide
sections.text: Quick Guide Wildfires can affect the ocean during the fire through smoke and ash, and again later when rain carries ash-enriched soil and contaminants downstream. Smoke and ash can reduce sunlight and deliver organic and inorganic particles. Nutrients can fertilize plankton, but large pulses can destabilize food webs or favor harmful blooms. Heavy metals, PFAS and other contaminants can enter aquatic food webs. Fire-suppression chemicals can add nutrients and contaminants to runoff.

sections.title: 1. Smoke & Ash
sections.text: 1. Smoke & Ash Wildfire smoke carries particulate matter whose composition depends on what burned. The source Field Note notes carbon, phosphorus, nitrogen, iron and heavy metals in ash, with urban fires potentially adding combustion products from plastics, fuels and other manufactured materials.

sections.title: 2. Sunlight, pH & Plankton
sections.text: 2. Sunlight, pH & Plankton Haze and suspended ash can reduce sunlight. Dissolved organic matter and nutrient inputs can alter bacterioplankton, phytoplankton and zooplankton responses, creating effects that can cascade through the marine food web.

sections.title: 3. Fire Retardants
sections.text: 3. Fire Retardants Fire retardants are useful for suppressing fires, but concentrated material reaching water can add nutrients such as ammonium compounds and may carry metals. Excess nutrient loading can contribute to poor water quality and harmful algal blooms.

sections.title: 4. The Second Pulse: Rain & Runoff
sections.text: 4. The Second Pulse: Rain & Runoff After a fire, winter rains can wash ash, nutrients, metals and other material from burned watersheds into streams and coastal waters. The biological result depends on the amount delivered, local conditions and which plankton species respond.

sections.title: 5. Kelp & Coastal Food Webs
sections.text: 5. Kelp & Coastal Food Webs KelpFire is a collaborative research program studying how wildfire-related materials affect California kelp ecosystems. The topic is important because changes at the plankton and kelp level can propagate through invertebrates, fish, seabirds and marine mammals.

sections.title: 6. Marine Mammals
sections.text: 6. Marine Mammals The Field Note identifies concerns including contaminant bioaccumulation, immune effects, prey changes, habitat degradation, stress and reproductive effects. It also emphasizes that marine ecosystems are complex and individual events may have multiple interacting causes.

sections.title: Guide Talking Points
sections.text: Guide Talking Points Visitor question:  Can a wildfire on land affect animals in the ocean? Short answer:  Yes. Smoke and ash can reach the ocean while a fire is burning, and later rain can wash nutrients and contaminants from burned land into coastal water. Those inputs can change plankton, water quality and the food web. Useful connection:  A coastal fire can produce two pulses—airborne deposition during the fire and watershed runoff after rain.

sections.title: 🦭 Seals & sea lions — symptoms & response
sections.text: 🦭 Seals & sea lions — symptoms & response The Marine Mammal Center 📞 415-289-7325 Report obviously injured, stranded or ill pinnipeds.  Do not approach or handle.  A resting seal on a beach is not necessarily stranded. Warning signs in the July Naturalist Field Note Excessive drooling or foaming, seizures, side-to-side head motion, disorientation, and unusual upward/backward head posture (“stargazing”). These warrant a call; do not diagnose from appearance alone. Keep observers and dogs well back. NOAA's stranding safety guidance says to maintain at least 100 yards when possible.

sections.title: 🦦 Sea otters — Monterey County
sections.text: 🦦 Sea otters — Monterey County Monterey Bay Aquarium Sea Otter Hotline 📞 831-648-4840 Report apparently abandoned pups, injured, ill or deceased sea otters in  Monterey County . Stay at least 50 feet away; do not touch, feed or attempt capture. Note exact location and behavior. Elsewhere:  Santa Cruz County and north, or San Luis Obispo County and south — Marine Mammal Center  415-289-7325  for live distressed otters. Dead otters outside Monterey County may be routed to CDFW. MBA stranded sea otter guidance ↗

sections.text: ⚠️ Oiled wildlife or suspected rabies Oiled wildlife 📞 877-823-6926 · Oiled Wildlife Care Network Do not attempt to clean an oiled animal yourself. Wild animal suspected of rabies Do not handle. For a living animal, call  SPCA Wildlife Center 831-264-5427 . If the animal contacted a pet or is deceased, Monterey County Animal Services:  831-769-8850 .

sections.title: 📍 Additional local contacts & situations
sections.text: 📍 Additional local contacts & situations Deceased whale, dolphin, seal, sea lion or turtle — Monterey County south of Pajaro River:  Moss Landing Marine Laboratories  831-771-4422 . Confirm routing with a wildlife responder if unsure. Dead seabirds:  NOAA advises leaving them in place on sanctuary beaches unless instructed otherwise; report unusual mortality events or suspected oil contamination. Roadside deceased animals:  Monterey County Public Works  831-755-4800 .
